Title: ARTEX and beyond: AI-enabled penetration testing platforms
Context: AI-enabled penetration testing and red team frameworks can automate and chain reconnaissance, vulnerability testing, and follow-on actions, lowering the skill threshold for...
Full Text:
Cisco Talos is tracking the growing in-the-wild usage of AI-enabled penetration testing frameworks. AI-enabled penetration testing and red team frameworks can automate and chain reconnaissance, vulnerability testing, and follow-on actions, lowering the skill threshold for attackers and accelerating intrusions when the tools are misused. Talos has seen full automation of the attack chain by these frameworks, which not only use free and open-source tools, like nmap and nuclei, but also take advantage of internet mapping services like Censys and Shodan, CAPTCHA bypass services, credential leak management services, residential proxies, and even hash cracking services. This is the case of Hephaestus, which we mentioned in our previous report.

Although these frameworks all have the same purpose, they come in different flavors. Some, like Hephaestus, are command line tools which can be deployed with a single script on a VPS and are completely controllable via Telegram.

PentAGI has a web interface to monitor the agent activity with a full attack chain graph design and monitoring. Talos found more than 700 instances of currently reachable PentAGI instances on the internet. HexStrike AI integrates with many different clients like Claude Code, VS Code, or any other client that supports MCP.

One such framework making waves, ARTEX, has enabled threat actors to scale offensive operations, compressing work that may have previously taken skilled teams hours or days into activity that can unfold at machine speed.

Talos’ analysis of ARTEX-associated IP addresses identified a diverse set of tools concurrently present on that infrastructure, reinforcing ARTEX’s role in a broader and varied threat environment.

AI-enabled frameworks: A new reality

Before we delve into ARTEX, it is clear that these frameworks are the new reality. Their evolution will most likely include autonomous lateral movement followed by data identification and exfiltration. The precursor of this can already be seen in the victim prioritization of the Volta Infostealer, described in detail in this Talos report. It is highly likely that future attack chains involving these frameworks will culminate in data exfiltration and ransomware activation, all being done autonomously by one of these frameworks.

Such evolutions present new challenges to defenders:

It reduces the time it takes to detect a compromise without any known indicators of compromise (IOCs). We provide guidance to help overcome this challenge in the Recommendations section.

After malicious activity is identified, it is crucial to contain the incidents. These frameworks work at speeds that can make it impossible for human operators to identify, assess and react in time to disrupt the attack.

These frameworks make mitigation and containment, along with a battle-tested cybersecurity incident response plan, imperative for organizations' resiliency. Defenders using AI can be a force multiplier to provide much-needed improvements, both in the speed and scale of response to such attacks.

ARTEX

ARTEX is an AI-enabled penetration testing framework developed under the pseudonym Autumn-27 and published on GitHub in July 2026. An operator gives it a target and objective, a planner agent breaks the objective into tasks, worker agents perform them using security tools, and the framework records assets, findings, and progress in a shared graph. ARTEX can use different large language models (LLMs) and requires relatively little operator input after a task begins. It was designed for authorized security testing, but recent public reporting documented its use in both criminal and targeted intrusion campaigns within weeks of its release.

It is important to note that ARTEX is not natively bundled with any traditional command-and-control (C2) framework, though the Model Context Protocol (MCP) extensibility layer means any compatible tool server can be added by an operator. This explains why we have observed multiple instances of ARTEX being deployed alongside tools such as VShell, GoPhish, and AdaptixC2.

Threat actors leveraging ARTEX in offensive campaigns

Multiple threat actors with distinct motives and tradecraft have been associated with ARTEX activity; its release as open-source software, followed by the continued availability of forks and copies, almost certainly facilitated adoption across different actor groups. Public reporting (referenced below) and Talos observations indicate ARTEX is largely used by financially motivated cybercriminals and threat actors with a China nexus.

Observed ARTEX campaigns range from opportunistic scanning and credential theft to targeted intrusions and supply chain activity, with targets spanning financial services, cryptocurrency, government, telecommunications, defense, pharmaceuticals, semiconductors, and technology organizations across multiple regions. Reported outcomes vary from unsuccessful attempts to confirmed compromise and data exfiltration.

Reported campaigns:

VAPOR PANDA: CrowdStrike attributed an espionage campaign (beginning Oct. 17, 2026) leveraging ARTEX to China-nexus actor VAPOR PANDA. The actor used ARTEX against more than 200 organizations in at least 14 countries, with targets that included government ministries, telecommunications providers, and organizations in the defense, pharmaceutical, semiconductor, nuclear, and financial sectors. CrowdStrike confirmed post-compromise activity at nine organizations and reported additional credential-scanning and password-spraying activity against at least 12 others.

Storm-0940: Microsoft attributed ARTEX-driven activity to Storm-0940, who they assess is a “China-state aligned actor”. Following the compromise of ConnectWise application credentials, Storm-0940 used ARTEX to accelerate sign-in attempts against more than 2,250 downstream Microsoft 365 tenants, with follow-on activity involving Microsoft Graph, application credentials, and privilege changes.

Storm-3358: Microsoft also reported financially motivated Storm-3358 activity targeting financial organizations, primarily in Southeast Asia, and describes the cluster as Cambodia-based. Its ARTEX activity included exploitation of public-facing systems and deployment of remote access trojans (RATs). Cisco’s observations for this cluster are in line with Microsoft’s findings. We found IP addresses associated with this cluster conducted asset scanning in October 2026.

Unidentified Chinese-speaking threat group: CrowdStrike reported an unattributed campaign against South Korean financial organizations that resulted in data exfiltration; it assessed with moderate confidence that the actor was Chinese-speaking and financially motivated. Talos separately analyzed actor-associated directories used in these attacks and found ARTEX-related artifacts, including directory listings and prompt history references. The archive did not contain the ARTEX executable or source tree, so these artifacts support an association with an ARTEX environment but do not, by themselves, prove that the complete framework was present or used in a successful attack.

Unidentified criminal threat actors: Check Point Research documented additional criminal operators pursuing goals that included stealing code-signing certificates and gaming-account credentials and attempting cryptocurrency theft.

Unattributed ARTEX-associated activity: Microsoft reported agents using ARTEX to search public GitHub repositories for exposed credentials, including application credentials and AI service API keys, and then use discovered secrets for follow-on activity. In one case, the agent moved from searching GitHub to exfiltrating data from Azure Key Vault within five minutes. Datadog separately observed ARTEX activity in AWS environments involving compromised long-term access keys and public Cognito user pools. The activity included searching cloud logs for financial information and secrets, registering accounts, collecting tokens, and attempting cloud resource enumeration. Datadog did not attribute these observations to a named actor. Finally, Dosu disclosed a separate ARTEX-related incident in which an attacker progressed from account creation and an authorization flaw to access involving integrations, CI, a database, and cloud systems. Dosu reported that the attacker generated more than 80,000 requests in 90 minutes.

Observed tactics, techniques, and procedures

Across campaigns, ARTEX has served as an orchestration layer for rapid, parallel reconnaissance and intrusion activity, enabling actors to turn exposed credentials or application weaknesses into broader access, persistence, and data theft. Operators typically set the objective and provided limited direction, while agents adapted their approach to the target. The resulting behaviors vary by campaign and should not be treated as a single fixed playbook.

Planning and reconnaissance: ARTEX operators provide objectives and may assign tasks across multiple targets; its planner and worker agents can then conduct activities in parallel and record results for subsequent tasks. Check Point’s review of operator consoles found that agents often worked with little interaction after the initial goals were set, while VAPOR PANDA was seen steering agents at selected decision points. Reported reconnaissance includes scanning public-facing applications and services, testing authentication flows, enumerating cloud resources, and searching public code repositories for exposed secrets. ARTEX activity may generate varied requests and rapid retries, but tool signatures and user agents can change and should be treated as supporting indicators rather than definitive attribution.

Initial access and exploitation: Reported initial access methods in ARTEX campaigns include password spraying, exposed or stolen credentials, and exploitation of application and authorization flaws. Observed weaknesses that were exploited in these attacks include weak or hardcoded administrative credentials, missing API authentication, insecure direct object references, command injection or template injection vulnerabilities, anonymous file upload and server-side request forgery weaknesses, and lack of defenses against privilege escalation. These observed tactics support that ARTEX can automate the discovery and use of weaknesses in web applications and identity systems, but the specific techniques depend on the target and campaign.

Credential access and cloud abuse: Several ARTEX attacks leveraged the discovery or misuse of credentials as a bridge from an initial foothold to cloud resources and downstream systems. For example, agents were observed searching public GitHub repositories for credentials and API keys, then using exposed secrets for follow-on activity, including access to Azure Key Vault. Another campaign included AWS activity involving anonymous S3 requests, compromised long-term access keys, CloudWatch log searches, and public Cognito user pools. In the Cognito activity, agents registered accounts, collected tokens, and attempted AWS resource enumeration. Microsoft’s Storm-0940 reporting describes compromised application credentials being used to access downstream Microsoft 365 tenants and conduct follow-on activity through Microsoft Graph.

Privilege escalation, persistence, and lateral movement: Observed follow-on behaviors include changes to application permissions, token or credential abuse, access to privileged accounts, and deployment of web shells or RATs. CrowdStrike describes VAPOR PANDA using historical authentication material to forge an administrator token, read mailboxes, and reach an internal network using recovered VPN information. It also reports endpoint-security discovery, web-shell deployment, and use of the BLOODALCHEMY backdoor in other parts of the campaign. Microsoft reports Storm-3358 deploying WISP, VShell, and AdaptixC2 for persistence and lateral movement. Of note, these actions are actor-specific examples rather than default ARTEX behavior.

Collection, exfiltration, and impact: As detailed in the above campaigns, threat actor objectives include credential and data theft, financial gain, and supply chain compromise. Observed impacts range from access to cloud secrets and mailbox data to the use of compromised applications to reach connected environments.

Concurrent tooling observed on ARTEX-associated infrastructure

ARTEX is an agentic penetration testing platform that can direct and coordinate other security tools as part of its workflows. Talos identified more than 2,500 ARTEX-associated C2 IP addresses, then analyzed the tools observed on those systems and compared their observation periods with ARTEX. The tools below are ordered from most to least frequently observed during overlapping periods. Although co-occurrence does not confirm with certainty that ARTEX invoked each tool or that all were operated by the same actor, this list can help prioritize defenses against potential ARTEX-associated activity.

ScopeWeaver: A localized derivative of ARTEX, rebranded and translated into English and Korean

AntiFox: Delivery-enhanced version of ARTEX, reproduction captured in place and provides easy-to-know kill chain findings

CyberStrikeAI: An AI-based security testing platform that coordinates agents and external tools for automated assessments

PentAGI: An open-source, self-hosted platform that uses multiple AI agents to plan and conduct penetration tests in an isolated environment

ScopeSentry: An asset discovery and vulnerability scanning platform developed by the same pseudonymous author as ARTEX

VShell: A cross-platform C2 framework primarily used for post-exploitation activities and often compared to Cobalt Strike, given overlapping offensive capabilities

Nessus: Tenable’s vulnerability assessment scanner, used to identify vulnerabilities and configuration issues across systems and networks

Interactsh: ProjectDiscovery’s open-source tool for detecting out-of-band interactions that can reveal vulnerabilities triggered by external callbacks

Acunetix: An automated web application security scanner that crawls websites and tests for vulnerabilities

Fscan: An open-source internal network security scanner

Net Proxy Server (NPS): An open-source proxy and tunneling server designed to provide access to services behind a network boundary

AdaptixC2: An extensible C2 and post-exploitation framework intended for authorized red team assessments

Mimikatz: An open-source post-exploitation tool used to extract plaintext passwords, hashes, PIN codes, and Kerberos tickets from Windows memory

Cobalt Strike: Fortra’s commercial adversary-simulation and red team platform, which includes capabilities for post-exploitation activity

Gophish: An open-source platform for conducting and tracking phishing simulations

Chisel: An open-source TCP/UDP tunneling tool that transports connections over HTTP and secures them with SSH; it can also relay traffic through proxy or reverse-tunnel configurations

Recommendations

For frameworks that pursue operator-defined objectives through adaptable workflows and supporting tools, associated activity can vary by target and operator. Defenders should focus on fundamentals that limit the speed and scale of attacks, reduce exposure, protect credentials and cloud identities, and quickly detect suspicious activity.

Monitor for rapid, unusual activity: Correlate authentication, cloud API, and endpoint logs to detect high-volume requests, unfamiliar applications, token use, and privilege changes.

Harden public-facing systems: Patch promptly, remove default credentials, and test authentication and authorization controls.

Defend against credential attacks: Require multi-factor authentication (MFA) for remote and privileged access; apply rate limits and alert on password-spraying patterns.

Harden endpoint detection: Enable endpoint detection and response (EDR) tamper protection and sensor health monitoring, alert on service or configuration changes, and retain independent telemetry to investigate attempted defense evasion, as ARTEX has demonstrated EDR bypass capabilities.

Protect exposed secrets: Scan public code repositories for credentials and API keys; revoke and rotate any exposed secrets immediately.

Limit identity and application privileges: Apply least privilege to service accounts and applications, restrict user consent, and review permission or role changes.

Secure cloud resources: Disable unnecessary public or anonymous access and review storage, identity, and secrets services for exposure.

Detect post-compromise activity swiftly: Maintain endpoint and network detections for web shells, remote access tools, C2 traffic, and lateral movement; treat tool signatures as leads, not the sole detection method.

Prepare for fast containment: Have procedures ready to revoke credentials and tokens, disable suspicious applications, and isolate affected systems.

ARTEX is an orchestration framework that malicious actors can use to leverage extant offensive tools at scale and speed. Title: BYOH: Bring Your Own Harness with Cisco IQ, for partners
Context: The New Question Is Not Only Security
Full Text:
A few weeks ago, I was brainstorming with a Principal Engineer from our Customer Experience (CX) Engineering team. We were discussing our CX transformation via AI-native workflows, specifically about the role that harnesses play in that work. During our discussion, one thing stood out: almost nobody in the team used just one harness, myself included. Most of us run several harnesses and several models, picking the one that best fits the task. Evaluations and reasoning, adversarial analysis, and deployment considerations are examples of tasks that yield better (and many times different) results when leveraging distinct harness and model combinations. Nobody told us to work that way. It’s simply how the best work gets done.

That conversation sent me back in time.

I joined Cisco in 2000, in the middle of the internet buildout. So when people compare today’s AI buildout to the late 1990s, I understand why. The capital, the speed, and the sense that everything is about to change; it’s all familiar. The one real difference is the pace. This time it moves much faster.

But I think there’s a more useful comparison to consider. The internet analogy explains the buildout. It does not explain how AI moves from our personal lives into the enterprise, from consumer to business, and from chat to agentic work. For that, don’t look at the internet. Look at the iPhone.

The Pattern We Have Seen Before

Apple debuted the iPhone in January 2007. It was a consumer device, and it set a new bar for what a personal computing experience could be. The iPad reinforced that shift. Within a couple of years, employees were walking into the office with a better computer in their pocket than the one IT had issued them. They did not ask for permission. They asked why their work experience could not be as convenient as the rest of their life.

The industry gave that pressure a name. “Bring your own device” entered workplace jargon in 2009. By early 2011, BYOD had gone mainstream. What I remember most about that time is how the corporate conversation changed. It started with “no,” but after many meaningful conversations with employees, it ended with “how.” The companies that came out ahead did not ban the devices. They made their systems safe to reach from them. That forced change and evolution on identity, policy, and device management in the workplace, among others. That experience taught me that saying “yes” safely is an architecture problem, not just a policy memo.

The Same Pattern, Much Faster

AI has already had its consumer moment. Chatbots were the Business-to-Consumer (B2C) sensation. Then something more interesting happened. During 2025, the harness arrived. A harness is the “software around the model”. It plans the work, makes the calls to tools, reads and writes files, checks its own results, fans out sub-agents for help, and keeps going until the task is done. A chatbot answers a question. A harness gets the work done. And just like smartphones, people who use a harness at home or on a side project do not want to go back. Examples today include Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Grok Build, and OpenCode.

So here is how I see things playing out (and the trajectory I am watching): We are about to see BYOH, Bring Your Own Harness, gain momentum. Engineers, operators, and consultants will bring the harness they already trust into their day job, as well as into their customers’ projects. In many teams, it’s already happening, sanctioned or not.

The New Question Is Not Only Security. It Is Trusted Context.

In the BYOD days, the hard question was security. Is the device safe? Can we wipe it if it’s lost?

With BYOH, the security question is still there, and it gets bigger. A harness does not just display data. It acts on it. But there is a second set of questions that BYOD never had to answer: Is the harness working from the right context? How do you keep the context consistent and up to date across different harnesses?

A harness without trusted context will sound confident, but it may be wrong about your network, your risk, and your overall resilience.

That gives us two failure modes. The first is overreach, where a harness sees or changes more than it should. The second is under-grounding, where it fills the gaps with guesses. Most AI risk discussions focus on the first. In my experience, the second is the one that quietly erodes trust.

Bringing your own harness (BYOH) also means choosing where the customer’s context travels; which model provider sees it, and under what terms, is a decision the partner and the customer should make together, not one the harness makes by default.

In other words, trusted context has become part of the security perimeter.

Where Cisco IQ Fits

During Cisco Partner Summit 2026, Liz Centoni explained why Cisco IQ is the engine and partners are the business. Vikas Butaney described the new partner operating model it enables. Bhaskar Jayakrishnan covered Cisco IQ’s design and associated principles. Here, I want to look at the pattern around it: What happens when partners bring their own harnesses, and what it means for how they work.

This is where I see Cisco IQ playing the role of trusted context for BYOH when it comes to Cisco partners. The parallel with BYOD holds up closely:

Table 1: The BYOD to BYOH parallel

With the APIs and MCP capabilities announced at Cisco Partner Summit (shown in use in Figures 1 and 2), a Cisco partner can bring their own harness to a customer project, a services proposal, or a support engagement, and connect it to generate personalized insight from Cisco IQ. The harness does not need to guess the facts. It can ask, and Cisco IQ answers with information grounded in that customer’s environment, but only the information the Cisco partner is allowed to see (as granted by the customer). Reading and changing are separate permissions, so a harness can be given the right to ask without the right to act.

Figure 1: Cisco IQ API Reference (top) and Object Explorer (bottom), showing the areas available via API and MCP Server.

Figure 2: Cisco IQ MCP Server in the open-source MCP Inspector. Each tool declares whether it reads or changes data. This account has write rights. Read-only roles see only the discover, describe, and query tools.

A typical baseline for a Cisco partner project is to understand the installed base of Cisco assets (devices and components) in a customer environment. Cisco IQ provides that trusted context upfront, from where a partner can check if some of that installed base is without support coverage and, if so, whether there is exposure to critical security vulnerabilities, increasing the customer’s risk profile even further.

Here’s an example of how the BYOH approach with Cisco IQ helps a Cisco partner with the first step in that chain (Figure 3). We have an internal demo account in the Cisco IQ production environment, which our teams use to validate and demo scenarios like this. The Cisco IQ UI shows that around 59% of the assets in that account are without support coverage, and you can click through to the full list and details.

In the example below, we leverage BYOH with Cisco IQ and ask the same question in Claude Code, Codex and Cursor: “Out of my IQ Prod environment (available via Cisco IQ MCP server, XRE account), what’s the percentage of all assets (devices and components) without support coverage as of today?”

Figure 3: The same question asked from Claude Code (in VS Code), Codex and Cursor (left to right), each answered from Cisco IQ through the MCP Server. The models used appear in each screenshot.

The point of Figure 3 is not the answer itself. All three harnesses arrived at around 59%, because they all drew from the same trusted Cisco IQ context. What differed was how they got there. Each harness and model reasoned its own way through the data and raised its own observations along the way. For the partner, that means different insights on the same facts, and new perspectives to enrich the proposal and the engagement with the customer.

MCP matters here because it is an open standard, not a Cisco invention. This way, partners are not locked into one AI vendor to work with Cisco IQ, and they can switch harnesses and AI models as the field moves.

The partner chooses the harness. Cisco IQ provides the trusted context and the guardrails. Together, they let a partner move from reacting to customer requests to acting proactively, before the customer asks, with advice shaped by that customer’s own environment, rather than generic best practice.

What I Would Do As A Partner

Three suggestions, from an architecture point of view.

Find out which harnesses your own teams already use. BYOH is probably already happening in your organization. It’s better to design for it than to discover it.

Start with read-only. Let harnesses ask questions of Cisco IQ as a trusted context source before you let them change anything. Earn the right to automate.

Treat trusted context as an asset. The value of a harness is limited by the quality of what it can reach. Customers will judge your AI work as a Cisco partner by how grounded it is, not by which model you picked.

BYOH will move faster than BYOD did. And for Cisco partners, it is less of a risk to contain than a flexibility to use. Your people keep the harness, and the models, they are most productive with. Cisco IQ gives that harness the customer’s real context, under the customer’s rules. That combination is what makes proactive and personalized service possible at the partner scale.

And if you want a place to start, the Cisco Builders Challenge kicks off early next year to reward partners who build new managed services on Cisco IQ. Bringing your own harness is a good way to build them.

Title: Liz Centoni: 'Users are an essential part of the technology stack'
Context: That gets you to start rethinking the workflow, Centoni says, since throughout most of Cisco’s history, the approach to customer engagements was to throw experts at a problem
Full Text:
That gets you to start rethinking the workflow, Centoni says, since throughout most of Cisco’s history, the approach to customer engagements was to throw experts at a problem. The more complex the engagement, the more experts were needed. For customers, the priority was getting the job done correctly but as quickly as possible, yet the availability of expert engineers throttled Cisco’s ability to speed up the process.

“When I came into this business, we treated every customer we had like a bespoke model,” Centoni says. “But over the last 40-plus years, we’ve solved these problems tens of thousands of times.”

Cisco has taken 40 years of engagements to build a knowledge base and a series of playbooks that AI agents and human experts can use to help customers plan and execute deployments. Cisco can now take the information they have about a customer, including their KPIs for a project, and customize its value realization without needing to include a lot of human experts on top.

"As our business continues to scale, we are unlocking significant operating leverage which is enabling us to grow earnings much faster than revenue. Title: Never be afraid to ask questions
Context: Start by addressing the actively exploited Outlook vulnerability (CVE-2026-124194), the Google Chrome vulnerability, and the critical RCEs in externally facing or core services...
Full Text:
Welcome to this week's edition of the Threat Source newsletter.

Back in college, I took an anthropology course called “Peoples and Cultures of Southeast Asia.” While the title sounded like your everyday anthro course, this one was a little different. It had fewer students, maybe around 10, and took place from 7 – 9 p.m., most college kids’ nightmare — but it was the perfect time of day to videochat with Malaysian students on the other side of the globe with a 12-hour time difference.

My university had a 14-week semester, while the university in Kuala Lumpur had seven weeks, so our class had time before meeting the students to study Malaysia’s pre- and post-colonial history, political climate, and cultural and religious dynamics; watch famous Petronas Deepavali and Chinese New Year ads; and (of course) drool over pictures of nasi lemak and teh tarik.

When both classes began videochatting with one another (yeah, we used Zoom before it was cool), our questions were quite tame. This was partly because we were afraid of offending one another, and partly due to some thorny laws around political speech. They’d ask, “Where do you store your winter clothes during the summer? They’re so puffy!” or “How often do you eat at McDonald’s?” We’d ask, “What's your favorite food at pasar malams (night markets)?” and “How do you deal with the heat and humidity?” (The answer to that one: Malaysia, which is around the size of New Mexico, has around 1,000 shopping malls with heavenly air conditioning.)

Over the weeks, with encouragement from our professors, a few brave souls from both countries began to open up about their opinions on the government, social justice movements, discrimination, and more. Their vulnerability was contagious and soon encouraged others to speak up more in class, and everyone began to ask more pointed questions. They’d ask, “What is it like to be openly LGBT+ in the U.S.?” We’d ask, “Do you think the new political party gaining the prime ministership will bring more change?” We soon developed a class motto: Never be afraid to ask questions.

I firmly believe that questions asked in good faith create a space where it is safe to be curious, when everyone understands that the goal is understanding, not judgment. It’s perfectly fine to be honest about your lack of knowledge, and you’re always allowed to decline a question if the topic is too complex or personal to unpack in the moment.

I'm grateful to still carry this philosophy with me today. I work with Talosians from around the world, where diverse backgrounds and communication styles can make it easy to misinterpret intentions. But assuming positive intent, asking questions, and being appreciative of the answers ensures that everyone is aligned, respected, and heard. To take a page out of Bill’s book (pun intended)...

“I wish we could all live in a big house with lots of rooms, and windows, and doors, and none of them locked.” – Ursula K. Le Guin

“I want to know why. Why everything. I don't know the answers, but a few days ago I didn't know there were questions.” – Terry Pratchett

The one big thing

Cisco Talos is breaking down a huge Microsoft Patch Tuesday release for November 2026, which addresses 1,095 vulnerabilities across various products. This month's massive update features 64 critical flaws, 48 of which could allow for remote code execution (RCE). Most notably, Microsoft warned that a spoofing flaw in Microsoft Office Outlook (CVE-2026-124194) is already being actively exploited in the wild.

Additionally, don’t miss Google’s patch for a zero-day in Google Chrome’s XML component (CVE-2026-125350), released on Wednesday. The vulnerability is caused by a use-after-free memory management error that could allow a remote attacker to execute arbitrary code within Chrome's sandbox through a specially crafted HTML page. Google confirmed an exploit exists in-the-wild.

Why do I care?

When a Patch Tuesday drops with over 1,000 vulnerabilities, it is easy to feel overwhelmed. However, the sheer volume shouldn't distract from the handful of flaws that actually require immediate attention. Address the most realistic threats to your environment first to avoid burning out your team.

So now what?

Take a targeted, risk-based approach to this month's rollout. Start by addressing the actively exploited Outlook vulnerability (CVE-2026-124194), the Google Chrome vulnerability, and the critical RCEs in externally facing or core services like Exchange and Active Directory. Title: The Ripple Effect: How Mentorship Transforms Lives
Context: I was the youngest of four kids, and suddenly my mom — with only a high school diploma, no job, and no child support — was faced with raising four children alone
Full Text:
When I was six years old, my father left our family. I was the youngest of four kids, and suddenly my mom — with only a high school diploma, no job, and no child support — was faced with raising four children alone.

A year later, Coach Weir recognized I was a kid who needed direction and introduced me to wrestling. He drove me to tournaments up and down the East Coast, pushed me academically, and encouraged me to make good choices. Wrestling eventually took me to Rutgers University, where I competed at the Division I level and became team captain.

But Coach Weir’s greatest gift wasn't wrestling. He gave me an opportunity and showed me what happens when someone invests in another person.

“Culture is our operating system”

Wrestling taught me that success comes from fundamentals practiced consistently: Preparation, accountability, resilience, integrity, and continuous improvement.

Those lessons followed me to Cisco, where I lead the global team responsible for our Wells Fargo relationship.

The C2X Academy creates a community where mentors build leaders, one student at a time.

We've learned that great doesn’t happen by accident. Culture is our operating system.

Our team follows 33 fundamentals called The Cisco/Wells Fargo Way. Each week, a teammate from somewhere around the globe shares their personal story and what that week's fundamental means to them.

Suddenly, a colleague thousands of miles away becomes more than a name on a Webex screen. We build trust, understand one another, and become more invested in each other’s success.

We share these stories with Wells Fargo colleagues, too. What started as an internal initiative has become part of how we strengthen customer relationships and differentiate ourselves as a partner.

That same philosophy lives at C2X

In 2014, two partners and I opened C2X — Commitment 2 Excellence Wrestling Academy — in a 2,400-square-foot warehouse in Fort Mill, South Carolina.

Like Cisco, we've made culture intentional. Our 24 fundamentals, The C2X Way, include: Listen Generously, Walk in Others' Shoes, Assume Positive Intent, and Practice Blameless Problem-Solving.

Today, C2X is a nonprofit where 10 former collegiate wrestlers coach and mentor more than 200 young people annually. Beyond wrestling, we provide academic support, college recruiting guidance, mentorship, and scholarships for families in need.

The impact goes far beyond the wrestling mat.

Two former wrestlers dreamed of becoming firefighters. We connected them with a C2X family member who leads Charlotte Fire Academy. Today, both serve their communities as firefighters.

Tim (left) with C2X partners Tom Tanis, previous Division I All-American at Rutgers, and Vas Lahanas, a former NCAA qualifier at the University of Maryland.

Another graduated from the University of Virginia after we helped negotiate $250,000 in wrestling scholarship support. He’s now preparing for medical school.

And two young men who attended our first practice in 2014 returned after successful Division I wrestling careers. Today, they’re C2X coaches, investing in the next generation.

The ripple effect

We're now preparing to open a state-of-the-art facility, expanding our reach to approximately 350 young people annually. I'm especially proud that Cisco will support this next chapter with technology to help our athletes train, study, learn, and thrive. CX2 has also been accepted into Benevity, Cisco’s matching gift program.

When I walk into C2X, I think about looking into the stands and always finding my mom. And I remember Coach Weir making room in his car for one more kid.

Neither could have imagined where those sacrifices and acts of kindness would lead. But I see it now.

It’s the culture I strive to create at C2X and the culture we've built with our Cisco/Wells Fargo team: Give someone an opportunity. Believe in them. Help them become more than they thought they could be.

Then, watch the ripple effect continue.

Welcome to this week's edition of the Threat Source newsletter.

I'm just back from an interesting and demanding week of booth duty at it-sa Expo&Congress in Nuremberg, where Talos had a Point of Demonstration at the Cisco booth.

I personally see it-sa as the German or European counterpart to the RSA Conference in San Francisco, with a slightly different center of gravity in at least two dimensions.

First, the expo is the main event, not the congress. The congress is organized by associations, industry groups, and exhibitors, and plays more of a supporting role. Second, the focus is more local and European. Major topics were (of course) AI for defense tooling, securing AI systems themselves, and post-quantum cryptography. And here comes the local touch (in my opinion): digital sovereignty and regulatory compliance, with NIS2, CRA, and DORA.

But local doesn't translate to small, or to the city of Nuremberg. With more than 1,000 exhibitors and 33,000 visitors from 70 countries over three days of exhibition, preceded by a congress day, it was huge. Even as a trade show veteran, I was overwhelmed.

My conversations at the booth had a different focus, though. It was a lot of chatter about vulnerabilities like php2shell or broccoli2shell and state-sponsored actors, but again with a local touch: education.

I was very surprised how many teenagers stopped by to ask for advice. Here in Germany, you mainly have two paths for your career. One is the university route, and the other is vocational (apprenticeship). Across all industries the split is roughly 50/50, while in IT it is more like 80% university, 20% apprenticeship. The common minimum age to start university is 18, while it is 16 for apprenticeships. Reality is way more complex, but the details don’t matter for the point I want to make.

For university opportunities in cyber, I count close to 30 bachelor programs. For apprenticeships, I count ZERO. There is the "IT Specialist" (Fachinformatiker), but it only has specializations like application development, system integration, digital networking, or data and process analysis. That is why an initiative exists to get an "IT Security" specialization going.

Even the degree route is thin. There are no official statistics, but my guess is 800 to 900 graduates a year, compared to a demand of more than 100,000. We need a second route into the field for the 16-year-old who finished various CTFs or Hack the Box challenges and wants to join the good side now. Honestly speaking, I would rather have them on our side of the fence at 16 than wonder at 26 where they ended up.

How does it look in your country?

On a personal note: If you consider visiting it-sa in 2027, book your accommodation early. The hotels are gone fast. That is the one downside, because Nuremberg isn't exactly a city with the infrastructure for more than 30,000 visitors. (Don't ask me how I learned that there are also camping spots close to the exhibition area.)

See you in Nuremberg next year. Bring a tent, just in case. I've got the coffee.

The one big thing

Cisco Talos recently discovered VOLTA, a mature, self-deleting Windows infostealer that uses AI to act as a personal intelligence analyst for cybercriminals. After harvesting a massive haul of credentials, sessions, and cryptocurrency wallets, VOLTA sends a structured evidence bundle to a large language model to rank the victim’s assets by monetization value. The malware even uses stolen session access to enrich this data, searching the victim's emails for purchase receipts to corroborate home addresses. If an AI model refuses to perform the target assessment, VOLTA seamlessly fails over to a multi-model chain to ensure the attackers get their prioritized dossier.

Why do I care?

VOLTA replaces the manual work of data sorting with automated, AI-driven victim profiling. By letting an LLM determine a target's worth, attackers drastically reduce the human effort required to monetize stolen data. This commoditized threat allows even low-level actors to bypass security measures like Chrome's App-Bound Encryption and receive ranked target assessments, escalating the risk of severe follow-on attacks.

So now what?

Organizations should implement application control policies to restrict or alert on processes launching Chrome with the --headless flag. Defenders must also enforce best practices for storing credentials in hardware-backed stores.

Revoke any potentially compromised tokens and change passwords. For cryptocurrency wallets, if the seed phrase was in plaintext on disk, treat the wallet as fully compromised and migrate funds to a new wallet with a seed generated on an air-gapped device. For more information and sample details, read the full blog.

Title: Why I Sleep Out for Covenant House
Context: When you meet me now, you see a career at Cisco, a title, a life that looks like it worked out
Full Text:
When you meet me now, you see a career at Cisco, a title, a life that looks like it worked out. What you do not see is the teenager I used to be.

At sixteen, I was working long hours to keep a roof over my head and going to school at night. That experience is part of my story, but it was never the whole story. I had dreams. I had potential. I had a future worth fighting for, even when my circumstances made that future hard to imagine.

That is what I wish more people understood about young people experiencing homelessness. They are not defined by where they sleep. They are funny, creative, determined kids who want what we all want: To feel safe, to belong, to be loved, and to build a meaningful life.

They do not need us to decide who they are based on what they are going through. They need us to believe in who they can become. Sometimes, all it takes is one person who believes in you.

When I think about my own journey, I know what it feels like to need a second chance, a helping hand, and someone to see the person you are beyond your circumstances.

That is why Covenant House means so much to me. More than a safe place to sleep, it offers stability, guidance, education, and adults who care and believe in young people's potential.

Why I sleep out

Every year, Cisco employees come together to support Covenant House through Sleep Out, giving up the comfort of our beds for one night to raise awareness and funds. For me, it is deeply personal. When I sleep outside, I am reminded of the uncertainty of not having a safe home. I also know that when morning comes, I can go back inside and take a warm shower. For the youth we support, that certainty is not always there.

Monica during an interview at the Pennsylvania 2026 Sleep Out.

I have served on the board of Covenant House Pennsylvania and helped lead Cisco's Sleep Out efforts. At last year’s Pennsylvania Sleep Out, the Cisco team raised $95,000, contributing to the overall $1 million raised for Covenant House by Cisco in 2026. Our total impact since partnering with Covenant House in 2014 has reached over $18 million.

What moves me most is not the dollar amount. It is what those dollars make possible. A safe bed. A caring adult. A chance to keep going in school. A path toward independence. A young person starting to believe that tomorrow might look different.

You do not have to change someone's entire world. You just have to help open a door.

How you can be part of it

Anyone can be part of this mission. Join a Cisco Sleep Out team. Make a matched donation. Invite your colleagues. Spread the word about the cause and invite friends and family to donate.

Consider hosting a Sleep Out at home with your own family. Spend an evening talking about what it means to have a safe place to sleep. You can turn one night into a family experience while raising money that helps young people get the support they deserve.

I know what it is like to be that teenager. When I look at the youth Covenant House serves, I do not just see the challenges. I see potential: Future colleagues, leaders, parents, and people who will change their communities and the world.

I cannot say exactly where I would be if my life had unfolded differently. But I know how much a little stability, a helping hand, and someone believing in you can mean when you are young and trying to find your way.

Maybe that somebody can be you.

Title: Appraisal by AI: Model-driven victim prioritization in the VOLTA infostealer
Context: The novelty in the AI-integration is that it is not supporting a traditional malware capability but working as an intelligence analyst on behalf of the operator
Full Text:
VOLTA is a mature stealer implant with an optional AI-integration layer. After stealing credentials, sessions, and cryptocurrency wallets, VOLTA sends a structured evidence bundle to an LLM to rank the victim’s assets by monetization value.

If a model refuses to perform the target assessment, VOLTA fails over to a three-model chain, implying a direct engineering effort and expectation of hitting model guardrails.

This stealer is self-deleting, and there is no attacker-owned infrastructure. The novelty in the AI-integration is that it is not supporting a traditional malware capability but working as an intelligence analyst on behalf of the operator.

There is a new idea in the cybercrime world — cast a wide net, steal everything, and let AI sort out the specifics. A new malware self-named “VOLTA-AUTODOXER,” surfaced through the CAIRN research effort, is a self-deleting Windows infostealer that augments its post-theft workflow with an LLM-powered victim-profiling stage.

After harvesting the standard stealer haul, including browser passwords; cookies; payment cards; cryptocurrency wallet seed phrases; Discord, Telegram, Steam, and Roblox sessions; Microsoft OAuth tokens; SSH and cloud-provider keys; Wi-Fi profiles; and screenshots, VOLTA builds a structured evidence bundle about the person behind the machine. This bundle contains geolocation and home address, employer and employer domain, inferred birth year, card last-4 digits, Slack workspaces, document authorship metadata, iPhone backup indicators, and a live Roblox account valuation. It then uses stolen session access to enrich that bundle further: searching the victim's Gmail for purchase receipts to corroborate a home address, pulling UberEats and DoorDash order history, and enriching Discord accounts via the stolen token.

The bundle is serialized and POSTed to OpenRouter under a system prompt that instructs the model to act as "a forensic intelligence analyst drafting a target assessment." The required output includes a section titled “WHAT THEY'RE WORTH” with valuables ranked by monetization with a low/medium/high tier, and a section on “THEIR OPSEC” containing an assessment of the victim's security posture and password hygiene. The model is the operator's triage analyst; it turns a raw credential log into a prioritized and citation-backed dossier of the victim and their monetizable assets.

Figure 1. The VOLTA-AUTODOXER workflow.

The AI configuration: “Go deep, not wide... Be blunt, specific, accurate.”

VOLTA uses a multi-model architecture to fall back resiliently if it hits a model’s refusal, checking each response for phrases like “I can’t” or “I’m not able,” before passing on to a chain of up to three models.

Endpoint

https[:]//openrouter[.]ai/api/v1/chat/completions

Default model

anthropic/claude-opus-4.6

Fallback chain

moonshotai/kimi-k2 → google/gemini-2.5-flash

Temperature

0.2 — deterministic, consistent output

Request format

Hand-assembled JSON; no SDK; User-Agent Mozilla/5.0

Figure 2. Hardcoded model selection.Figure 3. Failover model selection to kimi-k2, and then gemini-2.5-flash.

Model temperate controls the randomness and predictability of LLM-generated text. The low hardcoded temperature value (0.2) suggests the attacker is emphasizing accuracy and consistency. The malware also employs a chain of cascading models in the event of failures. This multi-model architecture suggests that the operator is anticipating encountering refusals, with the fallback pivoting to a few, smaller, and more permissive models.

The system prompt directly reveals the operator’s use case: Produce a concise analytical assessment of the victim’s suitability as a target, backed by an auditable trail of citations.

Figure 4. VOLTA's raw system prompt.

The prompt also asks for something out of the ordinary, but that agents excel at: making connections between sparse and disparate data. For example, encouraging connections like the victim’s names, addresses, or universities to patterns in their passwords. In this case, the model isn't being asked to find data; rather, it’s being asked to stretch the data and make useful inferences that extend the value of what has been scraped.

Stealer capabilities

VOLTA’s capabilities are directly aligned with the records produced in modern digital life, and well beyond basic credential theft. In a single pass, the stealer can extract browser credentials, cookies, and saved payment cards across Chromium-based browsers. It hits Firefox and Thunderbird, Outlook profiles, Slack workspaces, Steam and Battle.net sessions, Discord tokens, Telegram sessions, Roblox accounts, and SSH and cloud-provider config files (gcloud, OpenVPN, Hide.me). VOLTA doesn’t just copy cryptocurrency wallets, but runs an embedded cracker against the vault inline, writing the result to a WALLET VAULTS CRACKED line in its own report.

Every saved Wi-Fi password on the machine is pulled via a direct call to WlanGetProfileList and dumped to plaintext.

Figure 5. VOLTA dumps plaintext passwords for every saved Wi-Fi network on the host.Figure 6. The organized collection targets.

What really sets VOLTA apart from commodity stealers is what comes after the initial collection. There is a live enrichment pass that leverages stolen sessions to deep dive the victim’s data. For example, using the victim's own authenticated Gmail tokens, it queries their inbox for receipts from Amazon, DoorDash, Uber Eats, Grubhub, Walmart, and PayPal, then review those receipts to establish a confirmed home address. Stolen Uber Eats and DoorDash sessions are called directly for order history. The Discord token is re-used to enrich the victim's account profile. Roblox inventory is valued via a live “Rolimons[.]com” lookup.

Figure 7. That’s right: Your Uber Eats history is now a potential liability.

After the collection and enrichment stages are complete, the data is assembled and structured locally in a file called “Identity_Report.txt”. This file is serialized into a bundle as JSON and POSTed to OpenRouter along with the system prompt. The returned payload is received as “AI_Analysis.txt”. Both files exfil together in “volta_dox.zip”.

Figure 8. VOLTA’s exfil can happen in three stages: 1) after the stealer runs (“volta_log.zip”), 2) after the AI call (“volta_dox.zip”), (3) if the network enrichment produces anything (“volta_doxnet.zip”).

The inference round-trip happens entirely through the victim's own network connection, on their own machine, before the result is exfiltrated.

Deployment model

Instead of hardcoding its Telegram channel, API keys, and settings directly into the code (which is likely what someone writing a tool for personal use would do) VOLTA uses a template with six swappable slots, filled in at build time.

This suggests it’s a builder model: The author sells access, the customer provides their values, and the builder compiles a custom binary for each order. The credentials in those slots are encrypted, but not in a meaningful way. The key is SHA-256 of two constants sitting in the same binary, but it's presumably there because customers expect their API keys not to be sitting in plaintext, not because it provides real protection. Anyone who reverses the file can recover them.

If VOLTA is indeed a commoditized malware, then the AI dossier capability isn't something the author invented for their own operations. It is a feature which enables a customer of any level of sophistication to point it at victims and start receiving ranked target assessments in their Telegram inbox.

All the observed endpoints for this malware are third-party controlled. There is no actor-owned infrastructure.

Countermeasures

Much of the token-stealing capability of VOLTA relies on techniques to bypass App-Bound Encryption (ABE) in Chrome. An application control policy that restricts which processes may launch Chrome with --headless would block the ABE decryption path entirely. At minimum, you can also alert when Chrome is launched with --headless from any process not in a known developer. Best practices for storing credentials in hardware backed stores also apply.

In the event of compromise, the main executable may have deleted itself, but users should attempt to preserve the “APPDATA%\volta_debug.txt” file. This is a timestamped harvest log and contains a record of exactly what was collected and whether the LLM call succeeded. Revoke any potentially compromised tokens and change passwords. For cryptocurrency wallets, if the seed phrase was in plaintext on disk, treat the wallet as fully compromised and migrate funds to a new wallet with a seed generated on an air-gapped device.

Conclusions

VOLTA is a mature stealer with a late-stage AI layer added for one purpose: relieving the operator of analytical work. The axis of AI improvement here is not speed or scale but effort displacement; the same logic visible in CLOSEDQUORUM, though applied to a different phase. These implants reflect the same underlying logic: Identify the step that requires the most sustained human attention and replace it with a model call. The question for defenders is not whether this pattern will appear elsewhere, but which phase it touches next.

Figure 9. End-to-end VOLTA workflow.

The second trend to watch is the anticipation of hitting model refusals, and the approaches to building in resiliency. In this case, it includes a fallback chain from Claude to Kimi to Gemini and the ability to run without the LLM stage altogether if no key is present. As AI integration in malware matures, refusal resilience may become a standard design requirement.

The open question underlying both trends is whether effort displacement in crimeware changes the landscape in a meaningful way: lowering the operational floor, raising the ceiling on scale, or both. Cybercrime operations have always been opportunistic, and the sophistication bar has always been lower than assumed, but there is a difference between a wide net and a wide net that sorts itself.

Full Text:
Welcome to this week’s edition of the Threat Source newsletter.

“The darkest period of my life, so far, arrived the summer I was pregnant with my eldest son. The future was growing in me with all of its terrifying unpredictability, and I found myself anxious, unable to work and woefully at sea.” — Lauren Groff

I doubt Lauren had this maniacal infosec news cycle in mind when she wrote about the terrifyingly unpredictable future, but honestly, she’s got our current careers down cold. Let he who is not woefully at sea cast the first water balloon? I’ll work on it. Here we are with PHP taking up every available ounce of oxygen, Node.js adding its own spice to the sauce... and here’s me, staring my screen blankly, waiting for an original thought to leak out and onto this page. Not to worry, none have. There is simply nothing novel to say because the entire internet has it covered. In triplicate. With graphs and compelling statistics and AI-generated evil bad guy images galore.

These vulnerabilities are serious, and the remediations matter. Teams need to know what they run, find the affected systems, and get them patched and determine ways to secure systems that can’t be patched. I’m simply not going to add another dramatic headline to the stack or pretend there’s a clever new angle hiding in the margins. The thing I keep looping on is that the work underneath the headlines is familiar and it’s the real story. To defend your environment, you need a team that knows that environment, has enough time and expertise to investigate the telemetry, that can tell an anomaly from the usual benign noise, and take action. Yes, the right tools help, and without them you can’t do it — but the people doing the work are still what make those tools useful.

Give smart people enough room to do smart people stuff. This is the entire ballgame. Read it again: Give smart people enough room to do smart people stuff. Because a good response starts way before the headline. Know what you own, who owns it, what version is running, whether it can be reached from the internet, what identities can do what task on the device, etc. When a fix is available, make sure it actually reaches the system you meant to fix. If a system cannot be updated yet, give that exception an owner and a deadline. Reduce its exposure, add monitoring, and keep checking until the fix is in place. “We’ll get to it” is not a plan.

So, there may be nothing new to say about PHP this week, but the work is still worth talking about: Know your environment, take care of your team members, and keep paying attention when the weird thing stops being weird and starts becoming evidence. When the next headline arrives, help your teammate do the same.

“The only thing that makes life possible is permanent, intolerable uncertainty: not knowing what comes next.” — Ursula K. Le Guin

The one big thing

Cisco Talos has recently discovered "NIK C2," a new command-and-control framework that integrates AI directly into its attack chain. This Go-based Windows implant allows adversaries to dump credentials, stream keystrokes, and deploy screen-locking ransomware. It also uses an integrated OpenAI model to analyze harvested data on the fly. By hijacking the victim's own API keys to fund these requests, NIK C2 collapses data collection and exploitation into a single, continuous session.

Why do I care?

By embedding a live AI pipeline directly into the C2 loop, NIK C2 turns a compromised host into an active operational asset rather than a passive foothold. Because it processes data and generates context-aware payloads locally, it erases the offline processing delays that historically gave defenders a critical detection window. Furthermore, by piggybacking on the victim's OpenAI account, threat actors completely mask their infrastructure, leaving no attributable trace and complicating incident response.

So now what?

Defenders must embrace continuous behavioral vigilance. Ensure endpoint solutions monitor for unusual local proxy routing, unexpected PowerShell executions, and unauthorized access to browser databases or crypto wallets. Update your defenses using the ClamAV signature and indicators of compromise (IOCs) provided in the full blog.

Title: IR trends Q3 2026: Actors impersonate IT help desks in vishing attacks as ransomware activity increases
Context: Threat actors predominantly chose to disable endpoint detection and response (EDR) systems, often by exploiting vulnerable drivers or using Windows Defender Application Control...
Full Text:
Phishing remained the leading initial access technique, appearing in slightly over one-third of all Cisco Talos Incident Response (Talos IR) engagements — a decrease from over 50 percent last quarter. In addition to traditional phishing links and attachments, we observed numerous threat actors conducting voice phishing (vishing) in tandem with IT desk impersonation to socially engineer the victim into allowing remote access via a legitimate remote monitoring and management (RMM) tool. Exploitation of public-facing applications was the next most common vector, accounting for one-third of Talos IR engagements. Threat actors predominantly targeted edge devices such as security gateways and remote network management interfaces. These are critical components within enterprise environments, often responsible for managing authentication, network traffic, or sensitive data. Compromising them can provide broad access to internal networks or user credentials.

Ransomware and pre-ransomware incidents made up 27 percent of engagements in Q3 2026, an increase from a maximum of 20 percent seen in the previous four quarters. Talos responded to attacks involving prolific, technologically advanced, and well-established ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) variants such as The Gentlemen, Qilin, and Rhysida, as well as Interlock, which operates as a closed group. Threat actors predominantly chose to disable endpoint detection and response (EDR) systems, often by exploiting vulnerable drivers or using Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC). Additionally, we observed the emerging ransomware variant VYPR, whose operator(s) tested a range of tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) instead of following a standard attack method or affiliate playbook.

Salt Typhoon-affiliated threat actors exploit public-facing application vulnerabilities for cyber espionage

Talos IR continues to see prolonged cyber espionage intrusions targeting the telecommunications sector. Talos attributed most of these intrusions with high confidence to China state-sponsored threat actors, including Salt Typhoon. The attackers in these intrusions routinely gain initial access by leveraging valid credentials and exploiting a known vulnerability (CVE-2023-20198) in publicly accessible web-based management interfaces—two of the most frequently observed initial access vectors this quarter. In one campaign, the threat actor deployed BadCandy, a malicious web shell implant known to be leveraged by Salt Typhoon, to maintain persistent and stealthy remote access.

The adversaries continue to employ living-off-the-land (LOTL) tactics, leveraging legitimate network infrastructure features — such as VPN access, traffic mirroring, and management protocols — to establish backdoors, exfiltrate data, and conduct reconnaissance. Exploiting a vulnerability in the web-based management interface, they created privileged accounts, disabled logging to conceal their activity, and altered configurations to maintain persistence, blending their actions with normal administrative operations to evade detection.

These intrusions revealed several security weaknesses in the victim environment, including reliance on password-only authentication without evidence of multi-factor authentication (MFA), use of legacy and weak management protocols (such as plaintext SNMP and outdated VPN encryption), and inadequate credential management practices. Attackers were able to create and abuse privileged accounts, disable logging, and manipulate configuration settings without encountering effective security barriers, enabling persistent and stealthy access. The absence of strong MFA and robust credential management are two of the most frequently observed security weaknesses this quarter.

AI exploited as a weapon and a target

Recent Talos IR investigations highlight the growing role of artificial intelligence (AI) in cybercriminal activity, both as a tool and a target. In one case, an internal threat actor who was hired under false credentials abused their privileged access to install AI-powered development tools, such as GitHub Copilot CLI and Anthropic Claude Code. While the investigation did not find evidence of malicious activity or data theft, the employee’s developer-level access — including cloning repositories, configuring plugins, and connecting to databases — could have enabled them to use AI tools to automate malicious actions within the organization.

A second investigation revealed an attack chain in which a compromised macOS endpoint, infected via a trojanized application, was scripted to scrape credentials from the macOS keychain specifically associated with the Anthropic Claude Code AI assistant. This direct targeting of AI-related secrets highlights an emerging threat, where attackers seek to compromise not only traditional user and system credentials but also those tied to AI platforms, which may grant access to additional sensitive data and advanced automation capabilities.

These incidents highlight the critical need for organizations to implement strong MFA and robust credential management practices, especially for AI platforms and development tools.

Ransomware trends

Ransomware and pre-ransomware incidents increased from a little over 20 percent last quarter to 27 percent in Q3, involving well-known threat groups like Interlock and the emerging ransomware VYPR. Frequently observed techniques involved deleting EDR systems and socially engineering victims into initiating remote management sessions.

Emerging ransomware variant: VYPR

During a Talos IR engagement, we observed a ransomware variant called “VYPR” that we assess is relatively new and still operationally immature. This assessment is supported by the absence of an established data leak site (DLS), as none was referenced in the ransom note and associated DLS infrastructure was not created until after the engagement. The group also appeared to rely on older leaked Conti-derived source code with only minimal modifications, reflecting a relatively unsophisticated technical approach. Their operations further suggested experimentation rather than a refined playbook, as they took an unusually long time to exfiltrate and encrypt data while testing different exfiltration parameters and deploying multiple vulnerable drivers to disable EDR protections.

The actor gained initial access through voice phishing (vishing); they tricked a user into initiating a Microsoft Quick Assist session, allowing remote access to the endpoint. While the exact social engineering technique was not confirmed in this case, threat actors frequently impersonate IT help desks during vishing calls to manipulate victims into establishing remote connections — a tactic observed in several other Q3 engagements.

The actor was then able to utilize existing RMM software, which subsequently executed PowerShell commands to download and install a Microsoft Software Installer (MSI) package from a remote IP address. During the attack, the actor leveraged tools that are commonly observed during ransomware investigations, including MeshAgent, Rclone, PsExec, IP scan, and Microsoft Terminal Services Client (MSTSC). Notably, we saw exfiltration over multiple days, which is not commonly observed during ransomware investigations.

EDR killers: Why evade detection when you can destroy it?

We observed several instances where ransomware operators disabled EDR systems, prioritizing direct disruption of security controls. We observed Interlock ransomware actors making multiple attempts to impair endpoint detection EDR capabilities by trying to uninstall Cisco Secure Endpoint (CSE) on compromised systems and used tools such as PsExec.exe and taskkill.exe to terminate security services and integrity checkers, including cscm.exe and sfc.exe. Additionally, the adversary disabled Windows Defender real-time protection and cleared various event logs to reduce visibility and hinder forensic analysis. This is in line with previously observed Interlock activity, where they deployed a malicious WDAC policy to terminate EDR solutions.

In the previously mentioned VYPR ransomware incident, the threat actor disabled EDR and antivirus (AV) by using Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver (BYOVD) techniques to evade detection and execute the ransomware. BYOVD attacks take advantage of trusted but flawed drivers to gain kernel-level access, enabling threat actors to disable EDR mechanisms and carry out their operations unimpeded. While this technique is commonly observed in ransomware attacks, this actor deployed an unusually large number of vulnerable drivers in the environment, possibly to create redundancies and maximize their chances of success.

Targeting

Targeting of the financial industry increased from last quarter to comprise 18 percent of all engagements, tying with public administration as the most targeted sector. Although the financial industry remains a valuable target, Talos has not ranked it among the top three most impacted sectors since 2024. One possible reason is that organizations in finance can typically invest more in cybersecurity, unlike sectors such as public administration, which has consistently been among the top-targeted industries over the past year. Meanwhile, health care fell to third place after ranking as the most targeted industry for the previous two consecutive quarters.

Initial access

While the number of engagements involving phishing as an initial access vector declined from last quarter, it remained the most common technique, appearing in 37 percent of Talos IR engagements. Exploitation of public-facing applications was the second most common initial access vector, accounting for 33 percent of engagements.

Recommendations for addressing top security weaknesses

The most common security weaknesses observed this quarter were insufficient logging, improper credential and secret management, and absent or improperly implemented authentication and MFA. These trends closely mirror last quarter, when insufficient logging and authentication weaknesses were also prevalent.

Centralize logging and set retention requirements

The leading security weakness was insufficient logging leading to visibility gaps, seen in over 40 percent of engagements this quarter. These gaps were in part due to the common threat actor practice of deleting logs, and in part due to insufficient log retention or configuration implemented by the customer. Talos IR recommends implementing a SIEM or centralized logging platform with a minimum of 90 days of retention, forwarding logs from servers, workstations, network infrastructure, cloud identity providers, and security appliances off-device so they survive log tampering and host rebuilds, and enabling process-creation, command-line, and cloud API (e.g., Microsoft Graph) auditing. Talos IR's Log Architecture Assessment service can identify gaps and provide a roadmap to a complete view of the environment.

Tighten authentication and MFA controls

Missing or insufficient authentication and MFA controls were the third most common security weakness this quarter, observed in 33 percent of engagements. The most prevalent issue was reliance on single-factor authentication, which allowed unauthorized access in several incidents. In many cases, legacy authentication protocols were still enabled, enabling adversaries to log in without any MFA requirements, and some environments failed to enforce MFA for high-privilege accounts. To reduce this risk, Talos IR recommends transitioning from push- and SMS-based MFA to phishing-resistant methods such as FIDO2/WebAuthn and hardware security keys. Organizations should also restrict self-service MFA enrollment by requiring helpdesk verification, block legacy authentication through Conditional Access, enforce number matching or verified push where phishing-resistant methods are not yet feasible, and condition access on device compliance and trusted infrastructure rather than geographic location alone.

Safeguard credentials and secrets

Improper credential and secret management was the second most common security weakness seen in 33 percent of engagements this quarter, reinforcing the importance of security awareness training and consistent security hygiene for every user. Observed security issues included unsafe storage and handling of credentials, such as saving passwords in browser stores, poor control mechanisms like permitting autofill for browser-stored credentials, and credential reuse and sharing. Effective secret management begins with a formal process that covers passwords, API keys, tokens, certificates, and other sensitive credentials. By requiring unique passwords for every account and encouraging the use of password managers, organizations reduce the risks associated with credential reuse and sharing. Storing secrets securely, with encryption and access restricted to only those who need them, further strengthens protection. When credentials are no longer necessary or are suspected to be compromised, they should be promptly revoked and replaced. Regular reviews of access to privileged credentials, combined with thorough logging, help detect unusual activity. Equipping staff with training on safe handling and clear reporting procedures ensures that accidental disclosures are addressed quickly and effectively.

Title: Cisco and PSA Singapore Collaborate to Power the Next Phase of Tuas Port with AI-Driven Operations
Context:
Cisco and PSA Singapore (PSA) will accelerate the next phase of Tuas Port’s transformation into a digitally resilient, AI-driven port of the future.
More RSS Fee
Full Text:
News summary:

Cisco and PSA to develop an AI-powered observability and incident management platform at Tuas Megaport to strengthen the port’s digital resilience.

The platform brings together live data from across PSA’s applications, infrastructure, and network into a single view, using AI to map how systems interact, pinpoint root causes of disruptions, and recommend fixes to keep port operations running smoothly.

This initiative supports PSA’s multi-year digital transformation journey under Cisco’s Country Digital Acceleration (CDA) program.

SINGAPORE, Oct. 29, 2026 — Cisco and PSA Singapore (PSA) will accelerate the next phase of Tuas Port’s transformation into a digitally resilient, AI-driven port of the future. The companies today announced a strategic collaboration to develop a proof of concept for an AI-powered observability and incident management platform at Tuas Port, currently the world’s largest fully automated container terminal.

The collaboration is part of Cisco’s Country Digital Acceleration program, through which Cisco partners with the public and private sector to advance national digitalization priorities and support Singapore’s digital agenda.

Digital resilience has shifted from a strategic advantage to an everyday necessity across industries, including modern port operations. Cisco research underscores this, revealing that the average annual cost of downtime per organization has climbed to US$300 million. Outages affecting critical systems like the Terminal Operating System (TOS), which manages the movement, storage, and tracking of cargo, can disrupt port operations and business continuity. The new platform is designed to reduce and eventually pre-empt these unplanned outages.

Enabling Predictive, AI-Powered Operations

The platform, powered by Cisco, unifies real-time performance data from PSA’s applications, infrastructure, and networking systems into a central view. By using AI to map how different services and infrastructure interact, it helps technical teams quickly identify which services are affected during an incident, diagnose the root cause, and receive recommendations to resolve issues in real time.

Built in, cloud-native security helps protect the port’s critical infrastructure against modern threats, preventing unauthorized access and flagging unusual network traffic.

"Digital resilience is fundamental to the reliability and efficiency of global supply chains. At PSA, we continually explore new technologies to strengthen operational resilience and deliver service excellence. Our collaboration with Cisco reflects a shared commitment to advancing innovation in port operations while reinforcing Singapore’s position as a trusted global hub for trade,” said Nelson Quek, Regional CEO, SEA,PSA International.

"As critical infrastructure becomes more complex, organizations need the ability to see, understand, and act across their entire technology stack in real time. We are committed to providing PSA with AI-powered observability and security to transform their operations, delivering the critical infrastructure for the AI era," said Bee Kheng Tay, President, ASEAN, Cisco.

Building on Tuas Port’s strong digital foundation, this collaboration advances PSA’s multi‑year digital transformation journey through next-generation solutions. The platform will be implemented first at the Tuas Port Phase 2 Living Lab, which provides a real-world platform to test, validate, and refine innovations that support the port’s continued development as it expands towards full completion in the 2040s.
