Title: NIK C2: The new AI-enabled command-and-control framework
Context: NIK C2 reshapes adversary tradecraft by collapsing collection and exploitation into a single continuous session, effectively erasing the offline processing delays that...
Full Text:
Cisco Talos observed a new AI-integrated command-and-control (C2) framework in the wild called “NIK C2.”

NIK C2 contains a Windows implant, using which, an actor can dump credentials, stream the victim's keystrokes to collect the targeted victim’s sensitive data, and instruct an integrated AI model to analyze the harvested data, all within the compromised session.

In this framework, the actor has abused the OpenAI Chat Completions application programming interface (API), which is a HTTP endpoint that enables ChatGPT-style conversations programmatically.

In addition to the features that enable theft, an actor can also deploy desktop screen-locking ransomware via the NIK C2 implant onto the victim machine, leading to a ransom demand in Bitcoin or USDT cryptocurrencies.

NIK C2 reshapes adversary tradecraft by collapsing collection and exploitation into a single continuous session, effectively erasing the offline processing delays that historically granted defenders critical detection windows.

Such AI-enabled adversarial frameworks require defenders to move beyond traditional detection and embrace continuous behavioral vigilance as the new baseline.

NIK C2 implant: AI-integrated remote access tool

The NIK C2 implant is a Go-based, 64-bit Windows remote access tool that grants persistent control over compromised hosts using a resilient dual-channel C2 architecture. It communicates over TLS-secured WebSockets on port 443 alongside an HTTP fallback polling loop every 250 milliseconds, protecting all traffic with AES-256-GCM encryption derived from a hardcoded seed. To survive takedowns, the implant routes traffic across three prioritized C2 tiers, which are runtime-updated URLs, an embedded encrypted server list, and a hardcoded fallback address. Beyond standard operations, the implant features surveillance, theft, lateral movement, and evasion capabilities, including credential dumping, RDP session hijacking, process hollowing, and a C2-driven screen lock ransomware module.

Notably, the NIK C2 implant embeds a fully integrated OpenAI API client via its ai_generate command, allowing operators to route arbitrary prompts to the OpenAI Chat Completions API directly through the infected host. The NIK C2 implant manages API key resolution, request assembly, and response parsing locally, returning the encrypted generative AI results to the actor's C2.

The observed NIK C2 implant samples in the wild contains an embedded build path (/opt/nik_panel/data/build_52b79724a1fc4b8f/main.go), which identifies the project as "nik_panel" and indicates that the implant was cross compiled for Windows from a Linux development environment. Furthermore, the embedded eight-byte hex token matching the build identifier highlights that the threat actor's infrastructure actively tracking and versioning the implants.

Figure 1. NIK C2 implant’s operational architecture.

NIK C2 implant evolution timeline

Talos observed that the NIK C2 implant development trajectory spans at least three distinct versions. All binaries observed in the wild were compiled with Go 1.23.4 (which was released in December 2024), placing the entire sample set compiled no earlier than late 2024. The actor has Zeroed PE TimeDateStamp fields and near-epoch filesystem timestamps (manifesting as Nov 29, 1979) are applied consistently across all samples.

We developed a timeline based on the initial sighting dates of NIK C2 implant variants in OSINT.

Figure 2. NIK C2 implant evolution timeline.

The pace of capability addition across the three versions indicates a technically proficient team with prior malware operations experience is actively expanding NIK C2 towards a full-service adversarial framework.

Active NIK C2 server seen in the wild

During our research, we observed that a threat actor hosted the NIK C2 framework on a server at IP address “87.120.196[.]120”, resolving the domain “total-sitevv[.]lol”. The C2 server hosted an SSL/TLS certificate (serial number 7d16381a9de823943b5a0987dbd0f26edf22052b and jarm:"28d28d28d00000000042d42d0000001f361a1bf80ed39a1e352adeb016a07b" ) with the Common Name (CN) set to nik-panel. This CN value matches strings embedded within the implant binary. Observing the NIK C2 infrastructure active in the wild allowed us to assess with moderate confidence that NIK C2 is not merely a proof of concept, but a fully functional, AI-integrated C2 framework.

Figure 3. NIK C2 was observed in the wild during the research period.

NIK C2 implant integrates OpenAI’s API

AI integration is one of the most architecturally distinct features of NIK C2 implant. It constructs a fully formed HTTP request to OpenAI’s production inference endpoint, transmits it from the victim machine IP address, parses the JSON response, and returns the AI-generated text to the actor’s panel. The entire operation from receiving the actor prompt to returning the large language model (LLM) reply is executed synchronously with a 60-second timeout.

The implant begins by extracting three fields from the command payload received from the C2. The first field, identified by the key prompt, is the text the actor wants to send to the AI model. If the prompt string has zero length, the handler immediately constructs an error response and returns without making any outbound network call. The second field, identified by the key api_key is the OpenAI API key to use for authentication. The third field, identified by the key model, specifies which OpenAI model to use.

Figure 4. Snippet of NIK C2 implant AI handler module.

After extracting the three parameters, the implant checks whether the actor supplied an API key. If not, it calls the operating system's environment variable reader with the string OPENAI_API_KEY and uses the victim’s API key. This fallback is not a backup mechanism for API key resolution. It is a deliberate design with significant operational implications. If the victim has configured an OpenAI account on their machine, that account's API key will be used to fund the actor's AI inference. OpenAI's billing system will charge the victim's payment method, and OpenAI's access logs will show the victim's API key as the one that made the requests, allowing no trace attributable to the threat actor.

If the actor does not specify a model name, the implant falls back to a five-character default string stored in the binary data section. Decoding the five-character value showed gpt-4 confirming that GPT4 is the default when no model is specified. The actor can override this by passing any valid OpenAI model identifier in the command payload, allowing selection of newer models as they become available without requiring a binary update.

The implant builds the OpenAI API request body by constructing a map with four fields. The first field uses the key model and contains the resolved model name. The second field uses key messages and contains a two-element array of message maps. The third field uses the key temperature and contains a floating-point value read from a constant in the binary data section. The fourth field uses the key max_tokens and contains an integer value also read from binary.

The message array is constructed in the order that the OpenAI Chat Completions API expects. The system message is first followed by the user message. The system message map has the role system and a content string that is exactly 68 bytes long hardcoded in the binary. This 68-byte string is the implant's behavioral instruction to the AI. It defines the model's operational role and response style for the duration of the session. The user message map has the role user and contains the actor's prompt text verbiage. The complete map structure is then serialized to JSON. The JSON message is sent to the URL https:// api.openai.com/v1/chat/completions, the OpenAI Chat Completions endpoint, through an HTTP POST request.

Figure 5. Snippet of NIK C2 implant AI handler module.

When the HTTP response arrives with a 200 status code, the handler uses Golang's JSON decoder to parse the response body directly into a generic map structure without defining a typed schema. It then navigates the decoded map by string key lookups in the sequence that the OpenAI Chat Completions API response structure defines. The outermost map is queried for the key choices which in a successful response contains an array. The implant checks that this array is non-empty, then accesses its element keys message and content. The string value at key content is the AI model-generated text response.

After successfully extracting the AI-generated content, the handler assembles a result map with four entries. The key status is set to a constant string that reads as generated. The key code is set to the AI model's response text, so that the actor receives the full content of the model’s replies. The key model is set to the resolved model name that was used for the request, confirming which model produced the output. The key usage is set to the raw usage object from the OpenAI response, which contains the prompt token count, completion token count, and total token count. This usage data allows the actor to track how many tokens are consumed per request. The completed result map is ultimately transmitted to the C2 server over WebSocket or through the HTTP fallback C2 address.

Figure 6. AI model response is encapsulated in JSON message and will be sent to C2.

Dual execution modes of NIK C2 implant

Upon execution, the implant inspects its command-line arguments to determine its execution path. The argument watchdog activates supervisory monitoring to relaunch the core process if terminated, the copywatchdog tracks file copy operations, and the absence of either defaults execution to primary agent mode.

In primary mode, it uses a named mutex to enforce single-instance execution, logs a message reading [NIK] Starting, generates a 32-byte cryptographic session key if uninitialized, decodes its obfuscated C2 address, and sets its masquerade name to “svchost.exe” or “simvol.exe”.

After initial setup, the binary records its process ID (PID) in the victim's temporary application folder and executes its persistence and evasion routines. These routines include copying to %appdata%/Roaming/Microsoft/Network with modified access controls, configuring Windows autostart registry entries, and masquerading its process. Finally, it starts the local proxy server, initiates the WebSocket communication loop in a separate goroutine, and enters a continuous heartbeat polling loop on the main thread.

Implant’s C2 command surface overview

The implant command dispatcher module facilitates over 52 commands that are directed by the C2 panel. The dispatcher module uses byte-level string matching to map the associated modules that are launched as concurrent goroutines, allowing multiple operations to run in parallel.

Implant deploys screen-locking ransomware

The ransomware module of the implant operates as a multi-stage attack controller that the actor runs in sequence to prepare, deploy, and retract a screen-locking ransomware payload.

At first, it executes PowerShell to execute a raw disk copy command that reads directly from the physical drive device path (“\\.\PhysicalDrive0”) and writes the first sector, which is Master Boot Record (MBR), to a file named “mbr_backup.bin” in the Windows temporary directory.

Figure 7. Snippet of NIK C2 implant’s boot ransomware handler function.

Next, the module constructs a complete self-contained HTML lock screen code entirely at runtime from a hardcoded format string, parameterized with actor supplied Bitcoin and USDT wallet addresses, prices, contact email, timer duration, and custom text from the C2 command message, allowing the actor to fully customize the ransom demands.

Figure 8. Screenlocker HTML code is hardcoded in NIK C2 implant binary.

After generating the HTML code, the binary writes it to the file “lock_screen.html” in the system temporary directory. It then generates a Windows batch script that calls mshta.exe with the path to the HTML file, followed by an infinite loop construct with a five-second timeout between iterations, ensuring that if the user somehow closes the window it reopens within five seconds. This batch file is written to the temp directory as “lock_start.bat”.

The implant then runs a reg add command that writes a registry Run key named “SystemLock” under the current user's autostart path, pointing to a cmd /c invocation of the batch file, so the lock screen is executed on every user's logon. Additionally, a background goroutine is spawned that continuously monitors and relaunches the lock screen process. Finally, the module sends a confirmation response to C2 with the path of the deployed HTML file and the timer value.

The design of this ransomware module is notable for several reasons. It does not encrypt any files, which means it leaves no forensic trail of file modification timestamps or encryption markers. It relies entirely on a screen lock, which is considerably faster to deploy than a file encryption ransomware. The persistence via registry Run key and a self-healing loop ensures the screen lock survives user attempts to dismiss it and survives a system restart.

Figure 9. Desktop lockscreen page of the ransomware deployed by the NIK C2 implant.

Implant’s bootkit preparation feature

The bootkit preparation module of the implant is designed to survey the victim machine's boot firmware environment and then stage a bootkit payload file.

It executes bcdedit /enum, the Windows Boot Configuration Data editor, with the output flag that enumerates all boot entries while hiding the console window. The implant reads the full output and searches for three specific substrings in sequence including EFI, Windows Boot Manager, and Windows Legacy OS Loader. If any of these are found, the boot type is classified as UEFI. The binary also searches for ntldr, the legacy Windows NT loader used by BIOS-mode systems as a fallback. Based on which string was matched, the boot type is recorded as either "UEFI" or "BIOS" as a string of the appropriate length. Separately, the binary runs a PowerShell command invoking Confirm-SecureBootUEFI, which is a built-in PowerShell command that returns to the current Secure Boot state. The output is searched for the string True to detect an enabled Secure Boot and for False to detect an explicitly disabled Secure Boot. If neither is present, the value is recorded as unknown. The result is sent back to the C2, a map containing the boot type classification and the Secure Boot status string.

Then the implant writes a 16-byte placeholder file named “bootkit.bin” to the system temporary directory. The bytes written spell out "NIK_BOOTKIT_PREP" in ASCII, which serves as a staging marker rather than an actual bootkit binary. This placeholder confirms that the target path is writable by the current process, establishes the file location that subsequent operations will reference, and can be overwritten by the actual bootkit binary delivered through the implant's file-upload or file-write command handlers. The path to the staged file is returned to the C2 in response.

Implant’s theft functionality

When the actor issues the theft category commands from the C2, the implant executes the associated goroutines to collect the targeted data into a result map space in the victim machine memory:

WiFi password theft (wifi_steal)

The implant executes netsh commands directly via Go’s exec.Command function by passing arguments as discrete tokens rather than through a shell string. Harvested results are formatted under specific labels: plaintext Wi-Fi passwords appear under Key Content:, saved network names are cataloged under WiFi Profiles: (with missing entries flagged using the per-entry format [%s] not found), and execution failures or absent interfaces return standardized error strings such as [WiFi] no wireless adapter or access denied and No WiFi profiles found.

netsh wlan show profiles netsh wlan show profile name="" key=clear

Browser credential extraction (passwords, quick_steal)

The implant stages targeted browser database files into an archive alongside the Local State file, which contains the AES master key protected by Data Protection Application Programming Interface (DPAPI). The implant imports and executes the CryptUnprotectData Windows API to unwrap the AES key and decrypt the databases locally. Otherwise, it exfiltrates the raw encrypted databases to the C2 server for offline extraction.

Token and cookie theft (token_grab, quick_steal)

The implant extracts Discord tokens and session cookies from the levelDB store on the victim machine. The extracted outputs are labelled as === Discord Tokens === and DISCORD TOKENS. The browser session cookies (Discord_Cookies) are extracted from the copied Cookies database.

Cryptocurrency wallet theft (crypto_steal, wallet_export)

Victim’s desktop-based wallets are collected directly from the wallet storage paths. Browser extension wallets are extracted from chromium LevelDB stored by extension ID.

Seed phrase, private key file, and system reconnaissance

The implant performs two regular expression patterns to search on the entire filesystem of the victim machine. These two regular expressions are designed to scan file names for sensitive cryptographic assets and credentials, functioning as case-insensitive patterns ?i. The first expression targets cryptocurrency recovery materials and wallet backups by matching keywords like "seed," "mnemonic," or "wallet" paired with common plain-text and data file extensions (.txt, .md, .csv, .dat), while the second seeks out asymmetric private keys and general secrets using terms like "private," "privkey," or "secret" paired with both text files and standard cryptographic key containers (.key, .pem). Because both patterns use unanchored, greedy matching (.*) without start (^) or end ($) boundary anchors, they capture any file where these sensitive terms precede the target extensions. Matched data are collected under the label of seed candidates and archived into “browserdata.zip”.

(?i)(seed|phrase|mnemonic|recovery|backup|wallet).*(\.txt|\.md|\.csv|\.dat) (?i)(private|privkey|secret).*(\.txt|\.md|\.key|\.pem)

The implant also performs victim machine reconnaissance by executing the following commands and uses chcp 65001 prefix to force the output in UTF-8 format.

chcp 65001 >nul 2>&1 & systeminfo chcp 65001 >nul 2>&1 & wmic os get lastbootuptime /value chcp 65001 >nul 2>&1 & wmic /namespace:\\root\SecurityCenter2 path AntiVirusProduct get displayName 2>nul chcp 65001 >nul 2>&1 & Get-Process | Select-Object Id, ProcessName | ConvertTo-Json -Compress

After all collection paths are complete, the implant assembles all collected data into a single document that looks like a formatted report with clearly labeled sections for each data category such as === CRYPTO ===, === WIFI ===, === BROWSER ===.

Keylogger: Keystrokes livestreamed to C2

The keylogger module of the implant uses a persistent background goroutine that polls all 256 Windows virtual key codes, detecting keypresses via dynamically resolved API calls, and transmits the captured input. When a compromised victim presses a valid key on the keyboard, it is simultaneously streamed live as an AES-256-GCM encrypted JSON payload over WebSocket to C2 and also appends to an in-memory buffer capped at 10,000 entries and halved when full to prevent memory leaks. On an actor's dump command, this buffer is concatenated into a single string and returned to C2 via WebSocket or HTTP fallback, ensuring complete data transfer even during network interruptions.

Stolen data exfiltration to C2

Once the archive is assembled, the entire result map is handed to the result transmission routine of the implant. That routine constructs a new JSON object containing five specific fields. It includes the command identifier echoed back from the original command. It also contains the agent's persistent identifier, formatted as ag_<16 hex chars>. The type field is set to the string quick_steal_response. Finally, the data field holds the complete result map.

Once constructed, this object is forwarded to the encryption routine. The routine serializes the object into JSON. It then generates 12 fresh random bytes to serve as a nonce. Next, it encrypts the serialized JSON using AES-256-GCM with a static key derived from a hardcoded seed. It concatenates the nonce, the ciphertext, and the 16-byte authentication tag and Base64-encodes the entire payload. The encrypted payload is placed in a wrapper object under the "e" key alongside the plain-text agent ID, and the wrapper is JSON marshaled into the final payload.

This encrypted payload is then delivered through an available transmission path. The sending routine first checks whether the WebSocket connection is live. If it is, the payload is written directly into a WebSocket text frame on the existing connection, reaching the actor's panel with minimal latency. If the WebSocket is not currently connected, the routine falls back to an HTTP POST request to the endpoint path /api/c2/result on the C2 server, using the same encrypted body format. This dual-path design ensures stolen data is delivered even during WebSocket interruptions, as the HTTP channel remains functional independently of the WebSocket state.

Implant’s C2 protocol

The implant C2 architecture is designed for two independent, simultaneously operating communication channels. The primary channel is a persistent WebSocket connection over TLS. The secondary channel is an HTTP polling loop that posts to a fixed API endpoint at regular intervals.

With the primary channel, the connection begins with a TCP dial to the C2 server address with an eight-second timeout. If the port is not explicitly present in the configured address, port 443 is appended automatically. Once the TCP socket is established, it is wrapped in a TLS session using a custom certificate configuration that pins to a specific certificate rather than validating against the system's certificate authority store. This prevents standard TLS interception proxies from observing traffic.

Immediately after a successful WebSocket handshake but before any command is received, the implant transmits a full system registration message. The implant collects victim data such as the machine hostname, the local LAN IP address, the Windows username from the environment, a user security identifier, the local reverse-proxy port number that was assigned when the embedded proxy server was started, and the detected upstream proxy configuration derived from the Windows registry proxy settings. All of this is assembled into a JSON object and encrypted and sent to the C2.

Figure 10. Snippet of NIK C2 IMPLANT’s C2 communication handler function.

The HTTP polling channel runs independently. Every approximately 250 milliseconds, the agent collects a fresh snapshot of victim state hostname, watchdog status, local IP, username, current timestamp, and system uptime encrypts it in the same wire format and posts it to the /api/c2/update endpoint on the C2 server.

Below table shows the C2 endpoints that the implant communicates:

Endpoint

Purpose

/api/c2/update

/api/c2/result

Command output exfiltration

/api/c2/screen

/api/c2/file_chunk

/api/c2/rproxy_up

/api/c2/ws

Every message on both channels, in both directions, uses the same symmetric encryption scheme. A hardcoded seed value stored in obfuscated form in the binary data section is decoded at startup and produces a 32-byte AES key.

Decoded AES seed: d791dd0ff3228ed29a8d7333d4567be829159c5632ea347780992006f91c5295 32-byte AES key: 4887AFC0A574E9419A9695EF083460F58E4EF9A1C40793523CE112251273BDF9

The C2 server then responds with an encrypted payload, whose inner map contains a command array identical in structure to those delivered over WebSocket. Commands received through HTTP are dispatched through the same logic. If the HTTP POST fails, the agent rotates to the next server address before retrying.

Figure 11. Snippet of NIK C2 implant’s C2 communication handler function.

The result transmission to the C2 is performed by the implant when a command handler completes its operation, the result is packaged into a response envelope containing the original command's identifier, the implant's own identifier, a type string formed by appending _response to the command name, the result data payload, and a top-level type marker of "result". This object is encrypted and delivered through either directly over the WebSocket connection if it is active, or via an HTTP POST to /api/c2/result.

Implant’s defense evasion and anti-analysis techniques

The NIK C2 implant deploys a layered set of defense evasion measures that activate immediately at startup and operate across the full compromise session. On launch, It hides its console window via API ShowWindow, renames the binary to “csrss.exe” in the Windows temp directory to impersonate a legitimate system process, disables Windows Recent Documents telemetry through a registry write action, and applies a critical-process flag via API NtSetInformationProcess with the parameter value 0x1D for ProcessBreakOnTermination that causes a Blue Screen of Death if any attempt is made to terminate the process through Task Manager or taskkill actions.

Figure 12. Snippet of NIK C2 implant’s evasion handler module.

Alongside these, two anti-debug checks IsDebuggerPresent and CheckRemoteDebuggerPresent run silently and call os.Exit(0) on detection, leaving no exception record or crash evidence. When directed by the C2, the implant can also escalate privileges without a UAC prompt using the fodhelper.exe COM hijack, which writes the implant path into HKCU\Software\Classes\ms-settings\Shell\Open\command, triggers elevation, and cleans the registry key within two seconds.

The implant bypasses the Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI) by executing a hardcoded, embedded PowerShell script that patches memory inside “System.Management.Automation.dll”. Specifically, it overwrites the AmsiInitFailed field with a six-byte stub (MOV EAX, E_INVALIDARG; RET), forcing initialization to report failure and disabling content inspection for the remaining of the PowerShell session.

Figure 13. NIK C2 Implant’s AMSI bypass PowerShell script.

Conclusion

The emergence of NIK C2, an AI-enabled command-and-control framework, underscores a critical shift in modern malware design: the transition from static intrusion toolsets to dynamic, modular implants that adapt on demand. By embedding a live AI pipeline directly into the C2 loop, the compromised host is no longer a passive foothold but an autonomous operational asset. Operators can dynamically generate context-aware lure material, execute localized deception, synthesize operational intelligence, and craft targeted payloads directly on the compromised hosts — all while lowering the technical barrier which was traditionally required for such sophisticated tradecraft.

Title: Inside KeyDrift: Analyzing historical UAT-11473 activity on Cisco SD-WAN
Context: Cisco Talos has identified UAT-11473, a highly sophisticated advanced persistent threat (APT) actor, who exploited CVE-2026-20127, an authentication bypass vulnerability in...
Full Text:
Cisco Talos has identified UAT-11473, a highly sophisticated advanced persistent threat (APT) actor, who exploited CVE-2026-20127, an authentication bypass vulnerability in Cisco SD-WAN Catalyst Controller instances to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to affected systems.

UAT-11473 then installed a custom malware framework we track as “KeyDrift” consisting of multiple components geared towards collecting sensitive keying information, acting as backdoors and intermediate command-and-control (C2) hosts.

Observed targeting spans across space and satellite services, defense and aerospace technology, and policy research.

Talos assesses with high confidence that UAT-11473’s operating infrastructure overlaps considerably with Volt Typhoon’s “Silent Train” covert access network.

KeyDrift is a custom malware framework that is designed to operate in Cisco SD-WAN controller environments. Talos assesses with high confidence that the framework is designed to provide long-term persistent access and automated exfiltration of sensitive keying material. KeyDrift operates inside SD-WAN control-plane processes and is capable of intercepting decrypted control traffic, extracting control-session metadata and data-plane keying material, and staging or transmitting the collected material using encrypted records.

The framework's primary component is PolyFlame, a memory-resident module deployed through modified runit service paths. PolyFlame is injected into legitimate running vdaemon processes, and it can also masquerade as a packed “aaamgrd” loader variant. Once resident, PolyFlame interposes socket, DTLS, and runtime-linker behavior through functions such as recvfrom, sendto, getpeername, dlopen, dlsym, mprotect, and “/proc/%d/maps” parsing. This gives KeyDrift access to SD-WAN control-plane traffic from inside legitimate controller daemon execution rather than through a conventional endpoint beacon.

LittleFilch, another component of the KeyDrift framework, provides the collection and exfiltration capability identified in the framework. The module hooks “SSL_read” inside vdaemon, inspects decrypted control-plane buffers, extracts keying material for a list of predefined edge nodes, and stages the data locally in encrypted format for exfiltration.

Talos assesses with high confidence that KeyDrift's intended operational purpose is Cisco SD-WAN control-plane collection: persistent controller residence, in-band traffic access, key-material extraction from decrypted control messages, and encrypted staging or exfiltration of the recovered material. Observed variations of the KeyDrift modules and deployment mechanisms suggest active development of the framework’s capabilities.

KeyDrift analysis

KeyDrift uses Cisco SD-WAN runit service paths as its primary execution anchor. In the PolyFlame sshd deployment, the actor modifies the service run script, remounts /rootfs.rw executable, launches a malicious script “conf_sshd” in the background, and then starts the legitimate sshd service. The loader script enumerates running vdaemon PIDs, records them in “/tmp/system-vdaemon”, and invokes the injector component “rsshd” to inject PolyFlame (“libdssl.so”) into each process.

Recovered conf_sshd logic uses the same control flow across reviewed samples:

Figure 1. conf_sshd control flow logic.

Runit launchers

The observed sshd runit launcher preserves normal Cisco SD-WAN sshd startup logic while adding two malicious lines before service execution, which remount “/rootfs.rw” executable and background execution of conf_sshd, which then drives rsshd injection into vdaemon.

Figure 2. conf_sshd execution logic.

The recovered aaamgr runit launcher from an affected vBond appliance uses a parallel service-wrapper pattern, but it executes the packed aaamgrd PolyFlame loader directly. The deletion of the writable-overlay PAM configurations for sshd and login before remounting “/rootfs.rw” executable if part of the legitimate script, along with the invocation of the aaamgrd daemon via Python:

Figure 3. aamgrd daemon launch.

PolyFlame

PolyFlame is the primary operational module in the KeyDrift framework. PolyFlame operates at the socket and DTLS control-plane layer. PolyFlame serves two primary purposes:

Command execution via a TinyShell-styled backdoor

Intermediate C2 that can forward commands to and from the C2 to other peers

PolyFlame is primarily injected into the vdaemon process, providing operational obfuscation and access to all in-process state: DTLS session keys, vEdge topology, OMP routes, and policy tables. No hardcoded IPv4 addresses, binding ports, callback domains, URLs, host headers, or polling interval were recovered from the analyzed PolyFlame samples. PolyFlame is designed for in-band control or tasking over Cisco SD-WAN control-plane traffic rather than a conventional fixed external beacon.

This implant is meant to serve as a hook of the recvfrom() API call. The original recvfrom is replaced by a malicious subroutine in the vdaemon process. When recvfrom is called in the vdaemon process, the malicious subroutine will first execute the real/legitimate recvfrom() API to obtain the C2 IP address info for communicating with it in the future.

PolyFlame’s time check

The recvd data from the C2 consists of the MD5 value of a specific DATE. PolyFlame will calculate the local time on the device in format “%Y-%m-%d" and calculate its MD5 hash. If the MD5 calculated by the device does not match with the one sent by the C2, the implant will stop further execution. Otherwise, the implant then uses an “administrative code” from the C2 and performs an action.

PolyFlame’s tasking

PolyFlame contains an administrative mode that processes the admin code sent by the C2, that defines operations — it's one of the first flags checked in the backdoor:

Code = 1: Generate random bytes and send to C2. This is likely a check-in beacon or heartbeat for the C2.

Code = 2: Set implant type to backdoor (TinyShell) or intermediate C2.

Code = 3: Set up the command handler for the intermediate C2.

Any other code value: Check the implant type flag currently set. Based on the implant type flag, either send the accompanying data to TinyShell or the intermediate C2 component for processing.

PolyFlame’s command execution

PolyFlame contains a backdoor that matches the capabilities of TinyShell: file read, file write, and arbitrary command execution, but not interactive shell. This backdoor component’s implementation is quite similar to TinyShell, but the command codes differ. PolyFlame handles the following command codes:

Code = 0x100: Execute command using “/bin/sh -c <command>”

Code = 0x200: Write file to disk.

Code = 0x300: Read file from disk and send to the C2.

PolyFlame as an intermediate C2 component

The intermediate C2 component is a one-to-many handler (somewhat like a one-to-many multiplexer) — meaning the implant can connect to only one C2 but can connect to many peers who can be served by the intermediate C2 component. Similar to the TinyShell-backdoor component, the intermediate C2 component also accepts and processes specific command codes from the C2:

Code = 0x403: Create a thread to connect to the specified peer IP. Make a new connection and keep socket alive until specified.

Code = 0x404: Send data recvd from the C2 to a connected peer.

Code = 0x405: Remove a peer from the list of active connections.

Code = 0x407: Send a response recvd from a peer, back to the C2.

Code = 0x408: Set a specific value in memory.

PolyFlame variant: aaamgrd

Talos has observed a distinct PolyFlame variant that masquerades as the aaamgr service. The legitimate Cisco aaamgr component is a Python package; it does not normally appear as a compiled ELF runit service. This PolyFlame variant is executed by a malicious runit service under “/etc/sv/aaamgr/” with aaamgrd and a modified run launcher.

aaamgrd is a statically linked ELF64 executable with no section headers, a single RWE loader segment, and an RC4-encrypted embedded ELF payload. The loader uses direct syscalls including ptrace, fork, wait4, kill, tgkill, mmap, and mprotect. It performs an anti-debug check by deobfuscating /proc/%d/status and TracerPid: and exits if a tracer is present.

The observed staging sequence was:

Figure 4. PolyFlame staging sequence.

Note that in addition to the implant execution staging, there are also indications of timestomping.

LittleFilch: libcommon.so TLS interception module

LittleFilch is a control-session interception module positioned to collect data-plane keying material from control sessions visible to the injected vSmart process.

LittleFilch installs an SSL_read hook inside vdaemon. The hook calls the original SSL_read, then processes returned buffers only when the returned size is greater than 0x18F, the first decrypted byte is 0x07, and three marker patterns are checked for presence. These marker bytes are followed by the actual artifacts that LittleFilch aims to record:

LittleFilch records the extracted keying material and RSA-encrypts it before writing the output to “/var/tmp/vdaemon.bin”. It can then send the encrypted content over UDP in a DTLS 1.2 application-data style record.

Figure 5. Keying material recording format used by LittleFilch.

LittleFilch expects its configuration file — located at “/var/tmp/vdaemon.conf” — to contain two host port lines: one local bind IP/port and one remote destination IP/port. It deletes “/var/tmp/vdaemon.conf” after reading it. Talos has not been able to recover the “vdaemon.conf” file.

Recommendations

Cisco has released patches for CVE-2026-20127 and published a hardening guide for Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN deployments available here. Organizations are strongly advised to prioritize the application of these patches and follow the guidance provided.

Should any signs of unauthorized activity be detected, organizations should immediately activate their incident response frameworks. Title: Building a Career at the Biggest Company You’ve Never Heard Of
Context: The program offers a structured foundation for a sales career with internal mobility, and it provided the launchpad to a sales career I never imagined
Full Text:
I’d just finished business school at The University of Warwick when I joined Cisco in 2015 through the Cisco Sales Associate Program (CSAP).

This pathway wasn’t well-known among U.K. university graduates, but it’s a world-class early-in-career talent sales program at Cisco. The program offers a structured foundation for a sales career with internal mobility, and it provided the launchpad to a sales career I never imagined.

What’s CSAP?

CSAP is a three-month boot camp followed by six months of hands-on experience, and from day one, I was thrown into the deep end. I got to work with some of the U.K.’s biggest media clients as a Virtual Sales Account Manager, attending meetings about how Cisco enables some of the U.K.’s most famous TV programs and radio stations to thrive — including popular shows like “Love Island.”

After three years in Global Virtual Sales (GVS), including a stint as Team Leader, I transitioned into a Commercial Sales field role. There, I owned strategic engagements with major media clients and led a team of Virtual Sales Account Managers.

When the pandemic hit, I shifted focus to finance, legal, and high-end retail sectors, including some of the world-famous department stores in the U.K., such as Selfridges. Cisco fully supported my move by setting a flexible schedule that helped me balance learning with new responsibilities.

Stepping into my dream roles

I’ve always known I wanted to lead, and Cisco’s culture of promoting from within made that ambition feel achievable.

About three years ago, I stepped into my first leadership role, leading nine account managers across London and the southern regions of the U.K. and Ireland. This was the most excited (and nervous!) I’d been moving into a new role, but it was 100 percent the right move for me. My leader at the time really encouraged me to go for it and threw his support behind me. He helped me identify gaps in my skills and experience and worked closely with me on my development, something you often find here at Cisco.

GSX, Las Vegas, 2026. This annual sales conference provides the time to learn and connect!

Then, in December 2024, a role I’ve wanted since very early on in my career became available: Theatre Lead for Global Virtual Sales and Engineering, UK and Ireland. It was the role directly above the one I was currently in, and when I went for it, I made sure I took the advice of my Cisco mentors. In January 2025, I began the role, overseeing four First-Line Managers and a team of 31 Account Executives.

This is probably my sixth role within Cisco, and I’ve had the opportunity to work under seven or eight different managers, learning from each along the way. That’s why I’ve stayed at Cisco for so long — although it’s one company, the opportunity to learn, develop, and grow is immense!

Planning for your next career move?

For those looking to advance their career, my tip is this: It’s important to be proactive and honest about your ambitions with your managers. There are always options to pivot and grow. Leaders here understand that you won’t stay in one role forever, and that flexibility is key.

2026 Team Sports Day. A time to bond and enjoy some friendly competition!

I’ve experienced firsthand the incredible variety and the freedom to explore new roles, without ever leaving the company. If I ever feel ready for a new challenge or want to try something different, I know I can easily move to another role.

I also strongly believe that you’re in charge of your own career. My leaders have supported my goals, but ultimately, it’s up to me to take ownership. Cisco offers a wealth of internal resources for aspiring leaders, including self-guided courses on platforms like Mindtickle, Skills Studio, and LinkedIn Learning, as well as formal leadership training. The company also recently launched Time to Grow, which gives all employees four dedicated hours each month to build new skills and explore emerging technologies.

Another great thing about Cisco is the people you meet on your journey. Early on, I sought advice and connected with people across the business, simply by messaging them and asking for a coffee. Plus, I’ve made some of my best friends through CSAP and the wider company. I’ve been to Cisco birthdays, holidays, weddings, and even christenings!

Looking back, I’m grateful I chose Cisco over other paths I considered. The variety, culture, and opportunities here are unmatched. It truly is the biggest company you’ve never heard of, and I’m proud to be part of it.

Full Text: Cisco Partner Summit, Vancouver. #Sponsored by Cisco I attended Cisco Partner Summit this week, and during the global keynote, Tim Coogan, Cisco’s SVP of Global Partner Sales, said: “In 2018, there were more than two years between when a vulnerability was discovered and when it was exploited. Last year, it was about three weeks. This year, it’s eight hours or less.” Well, now if you only have eight hours, there’s no TIME to figure out your response after something happens, so leaders need to agree on their default actions ahead of time. Of course, Tim tied it to AI: “Customers cannot adopt AI until they trust the systems that run it.” Chuck Robbins, Chair and Chief Executive Officer of Cisco, talked about how “these agents don’t stop and go home and have dinner. They work 24/7, and there’s no limit to how many you can have working.” He was also clear about what customers are weighing: “Trust... takes years to earn and moments to lose.” I loved when Srini Namineni, Cisco’s Chief Automation Officer, asked the room to raise a hand if they had used AI in the last 24 hours, and pretty much everyone did. Then he asked people to keep their hand up only if AI had actually done something for them, like sending an email or booking a meeting, and about half the hands went down. In his words: “We’re used to getting answers from AI, but we’re moving to an era where AI can actually do things for you.” Getting an answer and letting AI act are very different decisions. Once AI is acting, we need someone to decide what it’s allowed to do and who is accountable when something goes wrong. He also shared that Cisco cut its partner support cases from 4 million a year to 400,000: “By fixing the root causes, we have reduced them by 90 percent.” Fix the reasons people open cases first, then use AI to close the rest faster. I’d recommend that order to ANYONE planning to automate a process. Liz Centoni, Cisco’s EVP and Chief Customer Experience Officer, started her talk with “Four days to 10 minutes.” A global insurer used to take four days to find out which of its 16,000 devices were affected by one security alert, and now it takes 10 minutes. Title: From federal SOCs to Talos: Ryan Fetterman on practical security research
Context: He shares the realities of detection engineering — including the creative, often frustrating ways attackers evolve their tactics to stay one step ahead of traditional defenses
Full Text:
What does it mean to be "blue collar" for the blue team? Amy sat down with security researcher Ryan Fetterman to discuss his journey from federal agency work to his new role at Talos. He shares the realities of detection engineering — including the creative, often frustrating ways attackers evolve their tactics to stay one step ahead of traditional defenses.Beyond the technical grind, Ryan shares his philosophy on building a career in security without burning out. From the value of project-based learning to the importance of finding time to step away from the keyboard, here's Ryan's take on what it really means to navigate today's cybersecurity industry.

Amy Ciminnisi: Tell me a little bit about the journey that has taken you to Talos, from early on in your career through to now. How did you get here? I actually don't know that much about it.

Ryan Fetterman: I've been doing security about 15 years now, and my career was largely shaped by where I started in the DC area. I spent about a decade there. I started out in consulting and then pivoted over to research, but that was a great place to get started.

I got a lot of great experience in federal agencies and government consulting, continued my education down there, got trained up, got certifications and things like that. And that was where I got my first exposure to doing actual security operations, which is what I really stuck with. It was my first exposure to Splunk.

Querying lots of log data and building visualizations and analytics in Splunk was the first time in my career that I felt it was kind of my natural inclination. It seems like it should have been more obvious to me looking back on it, but it's something that I try to explain to people a lot. When you first get into security, there's a desire to kind of find your specialization and start working towards it. But in my experience, it's just not something that you can rush.

I met the people connected with that space, which eventually led to me going to work for Splunk. I worked on the Splunk research team, SURGe. And then after the Cisco acquisition of Splunk, I ultimately became reorganized into Talos.

AC: I'm sure there have been so many challenges, so many obstacles in your way as you're trying to do this research. Can you share one that you've faced and how it shaped your perspective on cybersecurity?

RF: Something that stuck with me was actually my first advanced persistent threat (APT) incident. Now, you can look this up. It's called Pandora Song if you search for the C2. I was in the DC area working in a federal SOC, and I was doing some of the first host-based analytics at the time, which have now become kind of the concentration of a lot of detection. Engineering and analytics are host-based, so this was kind of pioneering at the time.

I was looking at a lot of host-based sensors and writing analytics in Splunk, actually, and we had been tipped off to this incident by a third party. I was looking through the details of the incident and how the attacker was carrying out the progression of their attack...

Title: Cisco Expands Partner Opportunity with New Cisco 360 Program Updates, High Yield Customer Experience Offerings, and AI-Ready Innovations
Context:

Full Text:
News summary:

Cisco introduces Ecosystem Deal Registration alongside new incentives and AI-enabled tools for partners to recognize and support our ecosystem at every step of the deal.

General availability of Cisco IQ for partners provides new profitability avenues and growth opportunities.

Expanded Cisco Cloud Control offerings provide partners with new ways to build, secure, and manage AI-ready infrastructure.

VANCOUVER, BC – October 26, 2026 – AI is moving infrastructure to the center of enterprise investment, creating a critical market opportunity to modernize, scale, and secure the networks that power the AI era. To help its partners lead this transformation, today at Cisco Partner Summit, Cisco (NASDAQ: CSCO) unveiled new advancements across its partner program, customer experience offerings and technology portfolio, providing the tools and incentives required to capture this next wave of global connectivity growth.

Expanded incentives within the Cisco 360 Partner Program combined with the general availability of Cisco IQ for Partners address the demand for more agility and intelligence in the current environment. Cisco Cloud Control continues to bring it all together, giving Cisco partners, IT professionals and AI agents a platform where they can work together to connect, protect and run the critical infrastructure for the AI era.

“Our partners are where Cisco meets the customer, and the AI era is asking more of all of us,” said Tim Coogan, SVP, Global Partner Sales, Cisco. "Customers need partners with the agility to move first and fast. By combining the strength of the Cisco 360 Partner Program with Cisco IQ and Cisco Cloud Control, we’re giving every type of partner new ways to deliver that and be rewarded for it, from the advisor who shapes a decision to the partner who delivers and supports it."

Powering an Agile Partner Ecosystem

Advisors, Developers, and Distributors increasingly shape what customers buy as well as how it's delivered, and as the Cisco 360 Partner Program enters its first full year, the program has added dedicated paths for each of them. Additional enhancements span program experience, profitability and enablement for all partner types, empowering true ecosystem agility in the AI era, and rewarding the contributions of every partner.

Ecosystem Deal Registration: A new way for Advisors and Developers to be formally recognized for contributions that lead to transactions, validating partner impact across the customer lifecycle.

New growth paths: Advisor and Developer Partner Value Indexes (PVIs) are now available and a new unified Distributor PVI will be available by Spring of 2027, underscoring Cisco’s commitment to measuring partner contributions based on the unique value their role brings to the customer.

Evolution of Cisco Partner Incentive (CPI) Rates: A continued investment in partner value exchange,increasing ACV growth reward by 50% as well as a 2x increase on Adopt for all use cases, as well as launching new adopt incentives on Cisco IQ.

Additional +2% Cross-Sell Bonus: An incremental +2% on top of the existing cross-sell rebate for Preferred and Portfolio partners expanding customer accounts into net-new Cisco architectures, including Splunk.

Cisco IQ Adopt Incentive: Designed to reward Partner adoption of Cisco IQ to ensure customers are onboarded and integrated with their telemetry.

Additionally, enhanced partner experience resources are now available to help partners differentiate and expand their offerings for customers:

Deal registration visibility in Partner Experience Platform (PXP): Automated, real-time insights to optimize pipeline health and enable partners to identify growth opportunities.

Advanced Trend Analysis and Eligibility Tracking: New PVI APIs enable partners to optimize their business outcomes and proactively manage their performance.

On-demand agentic resource: The One Cisco Content Agent (beta) makes it easy for partner sellers and marketers to quickly access approved Cisco content and customize value propositions for every customer tailored to specific priorities and industry trends, creating relevant co-branded presentations in minutes rather than hours.

New CPI Deal Estimator: Empowers partners to model deal economics and optimize rebate yield across every opportunity.

New OT certification: To reflect the growing convergence of IT, OT, and security, Learn with Cisco is launching a new Cisco OT Security Practitioner certification and releasing Cisco Modeling Labs 2.11 with new hands-on lab capabilities.

Cisco IQ: New Partner Opportunities for Profitable Services

Customers crave the ability to better understand their IT environments, intuitively identify risk, and quickly act before issues impact business outcomes. Partners need that same level of visibility so they can deliver more relevant, higher-value services to customers and propose modernization opportunities. Today, Cisco is announcing the general availability of Cisco IQ for Partners, empowering its global partner ecosystem to drive repeatable, high-margin growth across both managed services and reseller models. With more than 16,000 customers, and with visibility across close to 20 million devices since April 2026, the extension of Cisco IQ to partners provides new opportunities for growth after deal closure:

Deliver differentiated managed services: With Cisco IQ MCP Server and expanded API access, partners can seamlessly integrate intelligence into their own professional services, workflows, and AI agents. This enables partners to instantly query customer estates so they can address short term risks like emerging AI-powered threats, while helping customers plan for infrastructure modernization.

Secure, automated capabilities for Resellers: Through new Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) in Cisco IQ, customers can grant partners direct, secure visibility into their installed base. This transforms resellers into intelligence-led partners who can leverage real-time data and APIs to operate at machine scale—spotting hidden network risks, eliminating manual exports, and proactively driving customer modernization.

Cisco is also introducing new Cisco IQ capabilities for customers and partners:

New AI-Powered Quantum Safe and Software End of Vulnerability Support (EoVS)playbooks to help identify risks beyond routine patching.

Priority Bugs & Software Conformance Assessments to spot outage risks, prioritize remediation, and scope upgrades or hardening services.

Frictionless Cisco Cloud Control integration surfacing real-time risk intelligence, including quantum-readiness status, and enabling one-click action on at-risk, controller-managed devices directly within Cloud Control.

Cisco IQ AI Assistant enhancements based on rich contextual real-time data with troubleshooting now informed by device diagnostics and Cisco Technical Assistance Center (TAC) knowledge. Simplified TAC case management means you can create, close, and escalate a TAC case from within the AI Assistant.

"For too long, partners walked into customer conversations without the same view Cisco had. That changes today,” said Liz Centoni, EVP and Chief Customer Experience Officer, Cisco.

“With Cisco IQ Partner Support Standard, partners get that same intelligence under their own brand, delivered through their own experts. It's their name. Their customer relationship. Their services practice. Cisco IQ is the engine. Partners are the business."

Resilient, Secure, and AI-Ready Infrastructure Innovations

As enterprises scale AI agents across wired and wireless networks, they face mounting risks from downtime, visibility gaps, and identity-based threats. Cisco Cloud Control addresses these challenges by providing a shared, unified operations platform for teams and AI agents to secure and manage critical infrastructure across IT domains. To further enable machine-speed collaboration and automation, we are introducing new AgenticOps capabilities to Cloud Control, including:

Model Foundry:A new platform service in Cisco Cloud Control for putting Cisco’s purpose-built models to work — discovering, evaluating, fine-tuning, and running them on your own data, all in one place. Model Foundry is also the exclusive home of Cisco’s newest model versions and weights before broader release. Controlled Availability begins with Cisco partners.

ThousandEyes intelligence for trusted autonomous operations: Cisco is integrating ThousandEyes natively into Wi-Fi 6E and 7 access points, included with eligible Cisco Networking Essentials and Advantage licenses. With nothing additional to buy, deploy, or configure, always-on ThousandEyes enables automated background testing that is designed to validate application and network performance around the clock even when no users are online and strengthens customer trust in agentic actions.

Agentic integration: Cisco is introducing Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers for its networking platforms, which act as a standardized bridge that allows AI tools to easily access live network data. This removes the need for partners to build and maintain complex custom connections, making it simpler to create automated workflows for tasks like troubleshooting and reporting, while helping IT teams identify and resolve issues faster by linking deep telemetry directly to actionable experience metrics.

“The future of infrastructure operations is agentic, and it requires a platform that combines shared context, purpose-built models, and clear guardrails. Cisco Cloud Control is that platform,” said Jeetu Patel, President and Chief Product Officer, Cisco. “With the new Model Foundry, we’re advancing the state of the art in AgenticOps further. Enabling partners to fine-tune and customize Cisco’s models for their customers’ environments will make them integral to how their customers connect, protect, and run their infrastructure.”

To deliver the hardened physical and digital foundation required to connect, power, and protect mission-critical workloads for the long term, Cisco is introducing new resilient and quantum-safe innovations, including:

Extending quantum readiness across wireless networks: Cisco is launching the industry's first Wi-Fi 7 access point with quantum-resilient capabilities. This is the latest addition to the most comprehensive quantum-resilient networking portfolio, spanning wireless, switching, and routing, enabling partners to deliver quantum-readiness assessments and future-proof customer infrastructure investments well into the next decade. For quantum-safe communications with Post Quantum Cryptography over the air, Cisco provides Qualcomm Technologies-powered access points while the complete client-side solution is supported by an Intel Wi-Fi chipset and driver and Microsoft for Windows software.

Expanded support for Live Protect: Live Protect reduces the gap between vulnerability disclosure and patch completion on supported Cisco platforms and releases. Live Protect is now supported on N9000 Series Switches, N9300 Smart Switches, Catalyst SD-WAN, C9000 Series Smart Switches, and CW9800 Wireless Controllers. Support on Cisco 8000 Secure Routers and Cisco Firewalls is intended to be available by the end of 2026.

Privileged infrastructure access: Being developed in collaboration with Teleport, Cisco Privileged Infrastructure Access gives network teams and AI agents fast, governed, task-specific access to Cisco routers and switches, with short-lived, identity-bound certificates. Sessions are recorded, and privilege expires when the session ends.

Supporting Quotes

“Ecosystem Deal Registration is an important step forward in recognizing the value partners like Deloitte create throughout the customer lifecycle, from shaping opportunities and defining solutions to helping customers realize value. By making these contributions more visible, Cisco is creating stronger foundations for collaboration and shared growth.” -- Filipe Gomes Leonardo,Associate Partner - Cyber and Telecom Networks, Deloitte

“We are excited about Cisco's continued innovation and look forward to Cisco Partner Summit. With expanded partner access to Cisco IQ, we can build lifecycle integrations and professional services that turn reactive analysis into proactive insight. Together, we help clients manage risk, plan upgrades and get more value from every dollar they spend,” said Kevin Corace, Senior Vice President, Software and Services Lifecycle, Presidio.

“As our enterprise customers scale AI workloads and high-density wireless environments, the network must evolve from simple connectivity into an active, self-defending platform. Cisco’s innovations embed industry-leading security and continuous visibility directly into the physical infrastructure our customers need. Combined with NTT DATA’s Agentic Operations, this creates an intelligent operating environment that can sense, predict and act, proactively addressing experience degradation and securing mission-critical operations before disruption occurs.” – Dilip Kumar, President and Global Head Infrastructure Solutions, NTT DATA, Inc.

Cisco is increasingly tying together networking, security, collaboration, observability and services through platforms like Cloud Control and Cisco IQ. Why is that platform approach so important in the AI era, and what does it mean for partners and customers?

The platform approach [is] bringing simplicity, automation and speed. Everything that we're building, like with IQ, we're also building for regulated environments as well. No model is trained on that customer data. We don't train any of our models on that customer data because the telemetry is processed within a customer's bounded environment and never used to train our model. I wanted to cover that aspect outside of platforming because multiple deployment models are super important to us.

The [next thing,] if you look at what we've talked about, is open and API-driven. If you look at meeting partners and customers where they are, we're delivering that simplicity through open APIs and integrations with our ITSM partners. Rather than forcing partners into our own tools, as we do things like Cloud Control, we're delivering this enterprise depth. Same thing with IQ. We're doing cross-domain correlation across networking, security, and collaboration. These are the things that our customers need. Even if you look at services, when I came in, we had a confusing buffet of every capability [and] every kind of service that you could offer. We've streamlined this fragmented support program into three very clear tiers. There's a Basic tier, a Standard tier, and a Signature tier. I want to start with IQ because services is top of mind for our partners. I want to say [to them] that IQ is your new profit engine. As [partners] build their partner-branded-first architecture with what we're now making generally available, we're arming them with the telemetry and everything else. The second message is really around meeting partners where they are with open APIs and native integrations into ITSM providers. Then, we're backing it up with very clear incentive structures and enablement as well.

Title: I had plans for that second
Context: See an interview with Nick Biasini on php2shell defense: Top security headlines of the week 'PHP2Shell' Bugs Signal Red Alert for Security IndustrySecurity teams are scrambling...
Full Text:
Welcome to this week’s edition of the Threat Source newsletter.

Here for the latest on the PHP vulnerabilities? Head on down to ‘The One Big Thing’. Talos has published a blog to explain what we know so far, and details the Snort coverage available, including rules in the Community Ruleset.

But if you want a bit of levity, here’s what I wrote before everything kicked off yesterday:

Ever feel like the world is moving too fast to keep up? Well, I bring you scientific proof that it’s not just you.

For millions of years, the moon has been slowing down the Earth’s rotation. But over the past decade, we’ve been speeding up (I KNEW I was aging faster than before). Apparently, changes in the Earth’s core are involved (either that, or the 1978 Superman film was a documentary).

This is all causing massive headaches for the people responsible for keeping time. They’re officially called “The International Bureau of Weights and Measures”, but I’m going to call them “The Time-Keepers”. For nerd reasons).

The issue is that the atomic clocks that power so many of our systems, and the rotation of our planet, don’t always agree. Atomic clocks keep extremely consistent time, while each Earth day is rarely the same length as the next. Atomic timekeeping absolutely cannot stand that level of flexibility (have a watch of our “The Light We Keep” documentary to see the importance that accurate clocks have on critical infrastructure).

To keep Coordinated Universal Time (UTC), which is based on atomic clocks, aligned with Earth’s rotation, we introduced a “leap second” in 1972. This system allows for an extra second to be added, or taken away, when we stray too far from atomic time.

A few days ago, The Time-Keepers voted to officially abolish the leap second. Why? Well, there’s a few parts to it.

For the past 54 years, we’ve never once had a second removed from our lives. They’ve always been added (27 of them to be precise). I myself have experienced 20 of these extra seconds. If I’d have known that, I’d have used them more wisely. Like thinking before saying, “Love you too!” to the post-person this morning.

That added time, while it seems nice to have on the surface, can wreak havoc with our modern technology systems. In 2012, the extra second caused so much confusion that it crashed Reddit, among other systems.

The recent speeding-up of the Earth’s rotation complicates things further. If we keep going at this rate, it could result in the world’s first ever “negative second”. If you thought our technology systems struggled with added time, there are a lot of sciency brains who are very worried about the impact of taking time away. One of those concerns being… it’s never been done before.

So, what’s The Time-Keeper’s solution? Invent more time! Woooo.

Starting next May, the leap second will be replaced with a "leap hour," allowing UTC to diverge from Earth's rotation by up to an hour before a correction is made. None of us will get to experience that extra hour in our lifetimes, but our Great, Great, Great, Great, Great, Great, Great, Great, Great, Great, Great grandchildren are going to have one hell of a party.

For us current mortals, we’re all getting a little less time, and we’re hurtling through space a little faster. Happy Thursday!

But I guess I do want to make the point that I’m glad the risk has been thoroughly assessed ahead of, ahem, time. The Time-Keepers have decided that the world’s infrastructure should not have to find out how it handles a missing second by collectively experiencing one.

And I don’t even want to think about how all the AIs would cope with a negative second…

There’s something here for incident response planning. “It’s never happened before” is an excellent reason to test whether you’re ready for it. Run the exercise. Find out which part of your plan depends on something that, in this scenario, is also broken. Preferably before an adversary gets to supervise the practical demonstration.

Now, if only the Time-Keepers can abolish Daylight Savings Time next...

The one big thing

Two unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) flaws were discovered in PHP, rocking the internet. Dubbed "php2shell" and triggered by a simple HTTP request, this vulnerability affects every build since 5.4. Talos assesses that all industries running PHP applications are at risk for exploitation if systems remain unpatched.

Why do I care?

PHP runs WordPress, Drupal, Magento, Shopware, WooCommerce, and many other ubiquitous internet staples, so the possible blast radius is enormous. Older branches are end of life (EOL) and will not receive patches; these could account for around 50% of use cases.

So now what?

Cisco customers are covered with the Cisco Talos Network Intrusion Prevention (SNORT®) signatures 67359 and 67360. If your organization is running PHP 8.1 or older, Talos very strongly advises immediate update to PHP 8.2 or later. There is no patch for PHP 8.1 or older. See the article for more specific coverage and detection guidance.
